title: 25  Chain complexes, forms, and derived functors
text:
25.5 Resolutions

Definition 25.15 (Augmented complexes and resolutions) Let \(M\) be an object of \(\mathcal A\). A left resolution of \(M\) is a complex \(P\) with \(P_i=0\) for \(i<0\) together with a morphism \(\epsilon\colon P_0\to M\) for which the augmented complex \[
\cdots\longrightarrow P_2\xrightarrow{\ d_2\ }P_1\xrightarrow{\ d_1\ }P_0
\xrightarrow{\ \epsilon\ }M\longrightarrow0
\] is exact. It is a projective resolution if every \(P_i\) is projective and a free resolution if every \(P_i\) is free (Weibel 1994, Def. 2.2.4). Every \(R\)-module has a projective resolution, and every object of an abelian category with enough projectives has one (Weibel 1994, Lem. 2.2.5). A projective resolution of \(M\) is a cofibrant replacement of \(M\) in the model structure of Theorem 23.10, and the bar construction of Definition 23.5 produces one from the free-module adjunction.


Theorem 25.16 (Comparison of resolutions) Let \(\epsilon\colon P\to M\) be a projective resolution and let \(\eta\colon Q\to N\) be a resolution. Every morphism \(f'\colon M\to N\) lifts to a chain map \(f\colon P\to Q\) with \(\eta f_0=f'\epsilon\), and any two such lifts are chain homotopic (Weibel 1994, Thm. 2.2.6).


Definition 25.17 (Syzygies) Let \[
\cdots\longrightarrow F_2\xrightarrow{\ \varphi_2\ }F_1\xrightarrow{\ \varphi_1\ }F_0
\] be a free resolution of an \(R\)-module \(M\), so that \(\operatorname{coker}\varphi_1=M\). The \(i\)th syzygy module of \(M\) is \(\operatorname{im}\varphi_i\) (Eisenbud 1995, sec. 1.10).
A surjection \(F_0\twoheadrightarrow M\) determines its kernel; a free module surjecting onto that kernel is a further choice, and the resolution records the whole sequence of such choices together with the chosen generating family of each syzygy module.


Theorem 25.18 (The Hilbert syzygy theorem) Let \(k\) be a field and \(R=k[x_1,\dots,x_r]\). Every finitely generated graded \(R\)-module has a graded free resolution of length at most \(r\) by finitely generated free modules (Eisenbud 1995, Thm. 1.13).


Definition 25.19 (Minimal free resolutions) Let \((R,\mathfrak m)\) be a local ring. A free resolution \(F\) of \(M\) is minimal if \(\operatorname{im}\varphi_n\subseteq\mathfrak mF_{n-1}\) for every \(n\), equivalently if every differential of \(F\otimes_RR/\mathfrak m\) is zero (Eisenbud 1995, Ch. 20). For a finitely generated module over a local ring, and for a finitely generated graded module over a positively graded algebra over a field with its graded maximal ideal, the minimal free resolution is unique up to isomorphism, and every free resolution is the direct sum of the minimal one with a free resolution of the zero module (Eisenbud 1995, Ch. 20).
crumbs: 25  Chain complexes, forms, and derived functors

title: 25  Chain complexes, forms, and derived functors
text:
25.6 Derived functors, Ext, and Tor

Definition 25.20 (Left and right derived functors) Let \(F\colon\mathcal A\to\mathcal B\) be a right exact functor of abelian categories and let \(\mathcal A\) have enough projectives. For \(A\in\mathcal A\) choose a projective resolution \(P\to A\) and set \[
L_iF(A)=H_i\bigl(F(P)\bigr).
\] A second projective resolution gives a canonically isomorphic object, and the lift of Theorem 25.16 makes each \(L_iF\) a functor \(\mathcal A\to\mathcal B\) (Weibel 1994, sec. 2.4, Lem. 2.4.1, Lem. 2.4.4). For a left exact \(F\) and an \(\mathcal A\) with enough injectives, the right derived functors \(R^iF\) are defined dually from injective resolutions (Weibel 1994, sec. 2.5).


Definition 25.21 (Ext and Tor) For \(R\)-modules \(A\) and \(B\), \[
\operatorname{Ext}^i_R(A,B)=R^i\operatorname{Hom}_R(A,-)(B),
\qquad
\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(A,B)=L_n(-\otimes_RB)(A)
\] (Weibel 1994, Def. 2.5.2, Def. 2.6.4). Then \(\operatorname{Ext}^0_R(A,B)=\operatorname{Hom}_R(A,B)\) and \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_0(A,B)\cong A\otimes_RB\), and \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(A,B)=H_n(P\otimes_RB)\) for a projective resolution \(P\to A\) (Weibel 1994, sec. 2.6). Resolving either variable gives the same result: \[
L_*(A\otimes_R-)(B)\cong L_*(-\otimes_RB)(A)
\] (Weibel 1994, sec. 2.7). For projective \(A\), \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_n(A,B)=0\) for \(n\ne0\) (Weibel 1994, sec. 2.6) and \(\operatorname{Ext}^i_R(A,B)=0\) for \(i\ne0\) (Weibel 1994, sec. 2.5).
These vanishings are the hypotheses used in Theorem 19.16: for a lattice \(L\), projectivity kills \(\operatorname{Tor}^R_1(L,K/R)\) and keeps \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(L,-)\) exact on the sequence \(0\to R\to K\to K/R\to0\).

Weibel, Charles A. 1994. An Introduction to Homological Algebra. First. Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 38. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139644136.

title: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational
text:
Definition 28.2 (\(K3\) surface) A \(K3\) surface is a smooth, projective, geometrically integral surface \(X\) over \(k = \CC\) such that its canonical bundle is trivial, \[
\omega_X \cong \OO_X
\qquad\text{(equivalently } K_X\sim 0\text{)},
\] and its irregularity vanishes, \[
q(X) \definedas h^{0,1}(X) = h^1(X, \OO_X) = 0
.
\]


Remark 28.3 (The \(K3\) lattice) The integral cohomology \(H^2(X; \ZZ)\) of a \(K3\) surface is modeled by the \(K3\) lattice \[
\lkt = U^3 \oplus E_8^{2} = \latII_{3, 19}
,
\] the orthogonal direct sum of three hyperbolic planes and two copies of the negative-definite \(E_8\) lattice of the \(E_n\) lattice definition (Definition 36.6); it is even, unimodular, of signature \((3, 19)\). In the positive-definite (Euclidean) normalization for \(E_8\) this is written \(U^3 \oplus E_8(-1)^2\), the two descriptions denoting the same lattice. A marked \(K3\) surface is one equipped with an isometry \[
H^2(X; \ZZ) \iso \lkt
.
\]


Remark 28.4 (Hodge diamond) The Hodge numbers of a \(K3\) surface are \[
h^{1,1} = 20,
\qquad
h^{2,0} = h^{0,2} = 1,
\] with all other Hodge numbers vanishing except \(h^{0,0} = h^{2,2} = 1\); the Hodge diamond is \[
\begin{matrix}
&  & 1 &  & \\
& 0 &  & 0 & \\
1 &  & 20 &  & 1 \\
& 0 &  & 0 & \\
&  & 1 &  &
\end{matrix}
\] In particular the second Betti number is \(b_2(X) = 1 + 20 + 1 = 22\), matching the rank of \(\lkt\).
crumbs: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational

title: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational
text:
28.2 Enriques surfaces

Definition 28.5 (Enriques surface) An Enriques surface is a non-rational algebraic surface \(Z\) of Kodaira dimension \(\kappa(Z) = 0\) for which \[
h^1(\OO_Z) = h^2(\OO_Z) = 0
\] and the canonical class \(K_Z\) is a nontrivial \(2\)-torsion element of \(\Pic(Z)\).
Equivalently, Enriques surfaces are the quotients \(Z = X/\iota\) of \(K3\) surfaces \(X\) (the K3-surface definition (Definition 28.2)) by fixed-point-free involutions \(\iota\) — called Enriques involutions — and satisfy \(2K_Z \sim 0\) and \(q(Z) = 0\).


Remark 28.6 (Basic properties) 

Enriques surfaces are among the first examples of non-rational surfaces with geometric genus \(p_g = 0\).
They are minimal surfaces.
The universal cover of \(Z\) is the \(K3\) surface \(X\), and \(\pi_1(Z) \cong \ZZ/2\ZZ\) is generated by the covering involution \(\iota\), which acts freely and properly discontinuously on \(X\).



Remark 28.7 (Hodge diamond and cohomology) The Hodge numbers of an Enriques surface are \[
h^{1,1}(Z) = 10,
\qquad
h^{2,0}(Z) = h^{0,2}(Z) = 0,
\] confirming \(p_g = 0\), with all other Hodge numbers vanishing except \(h^{0,0} = h^{2,2} = 1\). The second integral cohomology carries a \(2\)-torsion summand, \[
\NS(Z) \cong H^2(Z; \ZZ) \cong \ZZ^{10}\oplus \ZZ/2\ZZ
,
\] and its free part is modeled by the Enriques lattice \(E_{10} = U\oplus E_8 \iso \latII_{1, 9}\), even unimodular of signature \((1, 9)\) (the Enriques-lattice definition (Definition 39.6)). Its \(2\)-twist \(E_{10}(2) = U(2)\oplus E_8(2)\) arises as the invariant lattice of the covering involution on the K3 cover; the Enriques period domain is governed instead by the transcendental lattice \(U\oplus U(2)\oplus E_8(2)\) of signature \((2, 10)\).
crumbs: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational

title: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational
text:
28.3 \(ADE\) and \(BC\) surfaces

Definition 28.8 (\(ADE\) surface) An \(ADE\) surface \((Y, C)\) is a log canonical log del Pezzo surface of index two whose boundary \(C\) has dual intersection graph a simply-laced Dynkin diagram (\(A_n\), \(D_n\), or \(E_n\)). These surfaces have canonical toric models determined by lattice polytopes in \(\ZZ^2\) (Alexeev and Thompson 2017).


Definition 28.9 (Priming) A priming is a weighted blowup at a boundary node (a corner blowup) that reduces the lattice length of a long edge. Allowed primings are restricted so as to preserve log canonicity and toricity (Alexeev and Thompson 2017).


Definition 28.10 (Folding) A folding passes from a simply-laced \(ADE\) diagram to a non-simply-laced \(BC\) diagram by taking the quotient by a diagram automorphism \(\tau\) (Alexeev and Thompson 2017; Alexeev et al. 2023). For instance \(A_{2n-1}\) folds to \(C_n\).
Folding identifies symmetric nodes, producing double bonds and merged nodes in the diagram. Geometrically, the surface is replaced by a quotient \(Y/\tau\): boundary components may become non-reduced, acquire multiplicities, or exhibit half-integral coefficients (half-divisors). Passing to the canonical double cover branched over the half-integral loci restores the integral \(ADE\) boundary.


Remark 28.11 The precise relationship between these foldings, the fixed-point subalgebras, and the orbit-sum construction (which can introduce a \(B/C\) Langlands duality) is discussed in the folded-root definition (Definition 51.3) and the Foldings section.
crumbs: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational

title: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational
text:
28.4 The base surface \(\PP^1\times\PP^1\)

Definition 28.12 (The base surface \(Y = \PP^1\times\PP^1\)) Let \(Y = \PP^1\times\PP^1\) over \(\CC\). The Picard group \(\Pic(Y)\cong\ZZ^2\) is freely generated by the pullbacks of hyperplanes \(\ell_1, \ell_2\) from the two factors. The intersection numbers are \[
\ell_1^2 = \ell_2^2 = 0,
\qquad
\ell_1\cdot\ell_2 = 1
,
\] yielding the lattice isometry \[
(\Pic(Y), \cdot) \iso
\left( \ZZ^2,\ \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \right)
= U
.
\] The canonical divisor is \(K_Y = -2\ell_1 - 2\ell_2\), of self-intersection \[
K_Y^2 = (-2\ell_1 - 2\ell_2)^2 = 8\,(\ell_1\cdot\ell_2) = 8
,
\] so that \(Y\) is a del Pezzo surface of degree \(8\).
crumbs: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational

title: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational
text:
28.5 The toric surface \(W\)

Remark 28.13 (The toric surface \(W\)) Let \(Y = \PP^1\times\PP^1\) and let \(\tau\colon (x, y)\mapsto(-x, -y)\) be the coordinate involution, which has \(4\) fixed points. The quotient \(W = Y/\tau\) is a singular del Pezzo surface of degree \(4\), with four \(A_1\) singularities. Both \(Y\) and \(W\) are toric, sharing the same polytope \[
Q_{4, 4} \definedas [0, 4]^2
,
\] but with different lattices: \[
M_Y = \ZZ^2,
\qquad
M_W = \ZZ^2_{\mathrm{ev}}
\definedas \theset{ (i, j)\in\ZZ^2 \mid i + j\in 2\ZZ }
.
\]
crumbs: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational

title: 28  Surfaces: K3, Enriques, and rational
text:
28.6 Moduli of elliptic \(K3\) surfaces

Remark 28.14 (The moduli space \(F_{\mathrm{ell}}\)) The moduli space \(F_{\mathrm{ell}}\) parametrizes elliptic \(K3\) surfaces with a chosen section, which fixes a hyperbolic summand \(U_1\iscontainedin\lkt\). The period map is defined on the orthogonal complement \[
T_{\mathrm{ell}} \definedas U_1^{\perp\,\lkt} \cong U^2\oplus E_8^{2}
,
\] of signature \((2, 18)\).


Remark 28.15 (KSBA and semitoroidal compactifications) Alexeev–Brunyate–Engel construct two KSBA (stable pair) compactifications of \(F_{\mathrm{ell}}\), each isomorphic to a semitoroidal compactification of the period domain (Alexeev et al. 2022):

Ramification divisor compactification \(\overline{F}^{\,\operatorname{ram}}\). The polarization is \([R] = 3(s + 2f)\), the ramification divisor of the double cover of \(\PP(1, 1, 4)\). The associated fan is a coarsening of the Coxeter fan.
Rational curve divisor compactification \(\overline{F}^{\,\mathrm{rc}}\). The polarization is \(R = s + m\Sum_{i=1}^{24} f_i\). The associated fan is a refinement of the Coxeter fan.

Geometric models for the boundary strata are constructed using integral-affine spheres with \(24\) singularities (\(\ias\)); see the singular-IAS definition (Definition 65.2). The Baily–Borel boundary contains a unique \(0\)-cusp \(\eta\) and two \(1\)-cusps, yielding the boundary lattices \(E_8^{2}\) and \(D_{16}^{+}\).





Alexeev, Valery, Adrian Brunyate, and Philip Engel. 2022. “Compactifications of Moduli of Elliptic K3 Surfaces: Stable Pair and Toroidal.” Geometry & Topology 26 (8): 3525–88.


Alexeev, Valery, Philip Engel, and Alan Thompson. 2023. “Stable Pair Compactification of Moduli of K3 Surfaces of Degree 2.” Journal für Die Reine Und Angewandte Mathematik 799: 1–56.

title: 29  K3 double covers and their involutions
text:
29.1 The double cover construction
This section records the general machinery of the K3 double cover of a rational surface, the distinguished geometric involutions it carries, and the lattice involutions they induce on \(H^2\) together with their invariant and coinvariant sublattices. The Coble-specific instance of the double-cover construction — where the base is a terminal Coble surface and the branch locus is the anticanonical curve — is treated in the section on K3 covers of Coble surfaces; here we develop the construction for a general base and the involution-theoretic apparatus common to the del Pezzo, Enriques, and Nikulin quotients. The general invariant/coinvariant lattice formalism \(L^G\), \(L_G\) is developed in the invariant/coinvariant-lattice definition (Definition 40.2) and the involution-eigenspace proposition (Proposition 40.3); we cross-reference it rather than restating it.
crumbs: 29  K3 double covers and their involutions

title: 29  K3 double covers and their involutions
text:
Remark 29.1 (The K3 double cover construction) A standard method to produce Calabi-Yau varieties involves taking a double cover \(\pi: X \to Y\) branched over a reduced divisor \(B\). If \(B \in \abs{-2K_Y}\), one takes \(\mcl = -K_Y\). The cover \(X\) is defined via the \(\OO_Y\)-algebra \[
\mca = \OO_Y \oplus \inverseof{\mcl}
.
\]
Adjunction yields \[
K_X = \pi^*(K_Y + \mcl)
,
\] and substituting \(\mcl = -K_Y\) gives \(K_X = \OO_X\), so that \(X\) has trivial canonical bundle.
Here \(\tau\) is the involution \[
\tau(x, y) = (-x, -y)
\] of \(Y = \PP^1\times\PP^1\), the involution covered by the Enriques and Nikulin involutions of the geometric-involutions remark (Remark 29.3); the del Pezzo involution covers the identity. Its fixed locus is the four torus-fixed points, those with \(x, y\in\theset{0, \infty}\). By taking \(B \subset Y\) to be a smooth \(\tau\)-invariant curve in \(\abs{-2K_Y} = \abs{\OO_Y(4,4)}\), we obtain a \(10\)-dimensional family of K3 surfaces, after quotienting by the toric automorphisms \(D_4 \semidirect (\CC^\times)^2\).


Remark 29.2 The specialization of the K3 double-cover construction (Remark 29.1) to a terminal Coble surface of K3 type is carried out in the section on K3 covers of Coble surfaces: there one takes \(\mcl = \OO_S(-K_S)\) for \(S\) the (rational) base and a section \(s \in H^0(\mcl^{\tensor_{\OO_S} 2})\) cutting out the anticanonical curve \(C\), and the resulting double cover \(f: X \to S\) is a smooth K3 surface with \(\Pic(X)\) a \(2\)-elementary lattice of invariants \((r,a,\delta)_1 = (10+n, 12-n, \delta)_1\) (Dolgachev and Kondō 2025 Prop. 9.1.1; Cossec et al. 2025 Def. 5.4.3).
crumbs: 29  K3 double covers and their involutions

title: 29  K3 double covers and their involutions
section: 29.2 Geometric involutions on the double cover
text:
29.2 Geometric involutions on the double cover

Remark 29.3 (Geometric involutions on the K3 double cover) For the K3 double cover \(X \to Y = \PP^1\times\PP^1\), there are three distinguished involutions acting on the coordinates \((x,y,z)\):

\(\idp(x,y,z) = (x,y,-z)\): the del Pezzo (deck) involution, the generator of the deck transformations of the double cover. Its quotient is a K3 quotient and \(\idp^*\omega_X = -\omega_X\).
\(\ien(x,y,z) = (-x,-y,-z)\): the Enriques involution, with smooth Enriques quotient \(Z\), satisfying \(\ien^*\omega_X = -\omega_X\).
\(\inik(x,y,z) = (-x,-y,z)\): the Nikulin involution, with singular K3 quotient \(Z'\) carrying \(\geq 8 A_1\) singularities, satisfying \(\inik^*\omega_X = +\omega_X\).

These generate a faithful representation of the Klein four-group \(\ZZ_2^2 \hookrightarrow \Aut(X)\). The del Pezzo and Enriques involutions act on the holomorphic \(2\)-form by \(-1\) (they are nonsymplectic), whereas the Nikulin involution acts by \(+1\) (it is symplectic); consistently with the group law, \(\ien\circ\idp = \inik\).
crumbs: 29  K3 double covers and their involutions

title: 29  K3 double covers and their involutions
text:
29.3 Induced lattice involutions on \(H^2\)

Definition 29.4 (Lattice involutions for K3 covers) Fix a basis of the K3 lattice \(\lkt\) corresponding to the decomposition \(U^3 \oplus E_8^2\), and write a general vector as \((u_1, u_2, u_3, \alpha_1, \alpha_2)\) with \(u_i \in U\) and \(\alpha_j \in E_8\). The three geometric involutions \(\idp\), \(\ien\), and \(\inik\) of the geometric-involutions remark (Remark 29.3) induce isometries of \(\lkt\), denoted \(\Idp\), \(\Ien\), and \(\Inik\) respectively, given in this basis by \[
\begin{aligned}
    \Idp(u_1, u_2, u_3, \alpha_1, \alpha_2)        &= (-u_1,\, u_3,\, u_2,\, -\alpha_1,\, -\alpha_2), \\
    \Ien(u_1, u_2, u_3, \alpha_1, \alpha_2) &= (-u_1,\, u_3,\, u_2,\, \alpha_2,\, \alpha_1), \\
    \Inik(u_1, u_2, u_3, \alpha_1, \alpha_2) &= (u_1,\, u_2,\, u_3,\, -\alpha_2,\, -\alpha_1).
\end{aligned}
\]


Remark 29.5 (Properties of the lattice involutions) 
The lattice involutions satisfy the following.

The group \(\generators{\Idp, \Ien, \Inik}\) is isomorphic to \(\ZZ_2^2\); in particular these involutions mutually commute, and \(\Ien\circ \Idp = \Inik\).
For each involution \(I_\star\), the invariant sublattice is denoted \(S_\star \definedas \lkt^{I_\star = 1}\) and the coinvariant sublattice is \(T_\star \definedas \lkt^{I_\star = -1}\), in the sense of the invariant/coinvariant-lattice definition (Definition 40.2): \(S_\star\) is the \(+1\)-eigenlattice and \(T_\star\) the \(-1\)-eigenlattice of \(I_\star\), and by the involution-eigenspace proposition (Proposition 40.3) these are orthogonal and rationally span \(\lkt_\QQ\).
The transcendental lattices \(T_Z\) of the Enriques surfaces \(Z\) primitively embed into these invariant sublattices.


The isometry classes of the invariant and coinvariant sublattices of the three involutions, together with their \(2\)-elementary invariants \((r,a,\delta)_n\) (where \(n = n_+\) is the number of positive eigenvalues) and discriminant groups \(A_L\), are collected in Table 29.1. For the del Pezzo and Enriques involutions these lattices also appear in Period domain embeddings and normalization alongside the sequence of primitive embeddings (Lemma 48.2). The Enriques (co)invariant lattices are built from the twist \(E_{10}(2) = U(2)\oplus E_8(2)\) (\(\sen = E_{10}(2)\), \(\ten = U\oplus E_{10}(2)\)), whereas the del Pezzo lattices \(\sdp = U(2)\), \(\tdp = U\oplus U(2)\oplus E_8^2\) retain an untwisted \(E_8^2\). The \(2\)-elementarity of both \(S_\star\) and \(T_\star\) is the content of the coinvariant \(2\)-elementarity proposition (Proposition 40.6), and their classification is Nikulin’s (Nikulin 1980).

text: 30.1 Numerical polarizations
crumbs: 30  Numerical polarizations and Noether–Lefschetz loci

title: 30  Numerical polarizations and Noether–Lefschetz loci
text:
Definition 30.1 (Numerical polarization) A numerical polarization \([h]\) on an algebraic surface \(Z\) — for instance an Enriques surface — is the numerical class of \(h \definedas c_1(\mcl)\) for an ample line bundle \(\mcl\in\Pic(Z)\), often written \([\mcl]\).


Remark 30.2 (Numerical classes on an Enriques surface) For an Enriques surface \(Z\) the first Chern class induces an isomorphism \[
c_1\colon \Pic(Z)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^2(Z; \ZZ)
,
\] so that the free part \(H^2(Z; \ZZ)_f\) is identified with the group of numerical divisor classes \(\Num(Z)\). Under the intersection pairing this free part is the even unimodular lattice of signature \((1, 9)\), i.e. the Enriques lattice \(E_{10}\) of the Enriques-lattice definition (Definition 39.6) (Cossec et al. 2025); the numerical polarization \([h]\) is thus an ample class in \(\Num(Z)\iso E_{10}\).


Remark 30.3 (Degree of a numerical polarization) The degree of a numerical polarization \([h]\) is its self-intersection \(h^2\) computed in \(\Num(Z)\). We are primarily interested in the degree-\(2\) case \(h^2 = 2\); the corresponding moduli space of degree-\(2\) numerically polarized Enriques surfaces is the space \(\fentwo\) appearing below.

title: 30  Numerical polarizations and Noether–Lefschetz loci
section: 30.2 The Noether–Lefschetz locus for Enriques surfaces
text:
30.2 The Noether–Lefschetz locus for Enriques surfaces

Remark 30.4 (The canonical cover and its involutions) 
The canonical double cover \(\pi\colon X\to Z\) of a degree-\(2\) polarized Enriques surface yields a K3 surface \(X\) carrying two commuting involutions: the fixed-point-free Enriques involution \(\ien\) (the deck transformation of the canonical cover) and the del Pezzo involution \(\idp\) (Alexeev et al. 2025).

Remark 30.4.1 The numerical polarization and the \(\Num\) marking are those of (Cossec et al. 2025); the canonical cover with its two involutions, the map \(j\colon \fentwo\to \fttz\), the locus \(\mathrm{NL}_{S_{\mathrm{En}}}\) and the KSBA-limit closure \(B\) are those of (Alexeev et al. 2025).



Definition 30.5 (Noether–Lefschetz locus \(\mathrm{NL}_{S_{\mathrm{En}}}\)) The moduli space \(\fentwo\) of degree-\(2\) numerically polarized Enriques surfaces embeds into the K3 moduli space \(\fttz\) via a canonical map \(j\). Its image is the Noether–Lefschetz locus \(\mathrm{NL}_{S_{\mathrm{En}}}\) defined by the primitive embedding of the invariant (algebraic) lattice of \(\ien\), \[
\sen = E_{10}(2) = U(2)\oplus E_8(2)
,
\] the rank-\(10\), \(2\)-elementary, signature-\((1,9)\) lattice of type \((10,10,0)\) (see the Enriques-lattice definition (Definition 39.6) and the Special Lattices section). The appearance of these extra invariant classes in \(\NS\) is what cuts out the locus.


Remark 30.6 (KSBA limits and non-normality) The Zariski closure \[
B \definedas \overline{j(\fentwo)}\iscontainedin \ksbacpt{\fttz}
\] parameterizes all KSBA limits of these double covers. The space fails to be normal along the boundary, due to branching and boundary divisor intersections.

title: 30  Numerical polarizations and Noether–Lefschetz loci
section: 30.3 Two polarization classes on a Coble surface
text:
30.3 Two polarization classes on a Coble surface

Remark 30.7 On the K3 cover of a Coble surface with \(n = 1\) there are two distinct divisor classes of square \(2\), and the K3 cover, and a third class of square \(4\); keeping them apart is what makes the comparison with \(F_{\En, 2}\) well posed. Throughout, \(S = \Bl_{p_1,\dots,p_{10}}\PP^2\) is the ten-point blowup, \(\Pic(S) = \generators{H, E_1,\dots,E_{10}}\cong\latI_{1,10}\) is its Picard lattice with \(H^2 = 1\), \(E_i^2 = -1\) and \(H\cdot E_i = E_i\cdot E_j = 0\) for \(i\neq j\), and \(f\colon X\to S\) is the K3 double cover.


Proposition 30.8 (The canonical complement is the Enriques lattice) In \(\Pic(S)\cong\latI_{1,10}\) one has \(K_S = -3H + \Sum_{i=1}^{10} E_i\), and a divisor \(D = aH - \Sum_i b_i E_i\) lies in \(K_S^{\perp}\) if and only if \[
\Sum_{i=1}^{10} b_i = 3a
.
\] The sublattice \(K_S^{\perp}\) is even and unimodular of signature \((1, 9)\), hence \[
K_S^{\perp} \cong E_{10} = U\oplus E_8
,
\] the Enriques lattice of the Enriques-lattice definition (Definition 39.6). The Coble boundary curve has class \[
C = 6H - 2\Sum_{i=1}^{10} E_i = -2K_S
.
\]


Proof. The expression for \(K_S\) is the blowup formula, and \(D\cdot K_S = -3a - \Sum_i(-b_i)(-1)\cdot(-1)\) evaluates to \(3a - \Sum_i b_i\) up to sign, giving the stated condition. Since \(K_S^2 = 9 - 10 = -1\), the rank-one sublattice \(\generators{K_S}\cong\generators{-1}\) is unimodular, so by the unimodular-splitting proposition (Proposition 38.12) it splits \(\Pic(S)\) and its complement \(K_S^{\perp}\) is unimodular of signature \((1, 9)\). That complement is even: for \(D = aH - \Sum_i b_iE_i\) with \(\Sum_i b_i = 3a\), \[
D^2 = a^2 - \Sum_i b_i^2 \equiv a^2 - \Sum_i b_i = a^2 - 3a \equiv a(a-1) \equiv 0
\pmod 2
,
\] using \(b^2\equiv b\bmod 2\). An even unimodular lattice of signature \((1,9)\) is isometric to \(E_{10}\) by the indefinite unimodular classification (Theorem 38.20). Finally \(C = -2K_S = 6H - 2\Sum_i E_i\) by the description of \(K_S\).


Definition 30.9 (The plane class and the degree-\(2\) Coble polarization) 
The two classes to be distinguished are:

the plane class \(H\in\Pic(S)\), the pullback of a line, with \(H^2 = 1\); its K3 pullback \(e_0\definedas f^{*}H\in S_\Co\) has \(e_0^2 = 2\) by the K3 double-cover proposition (Proposition 32.2);
the degree-\(2\) Coble polarization \(h_\Co\in K_S^{\perp}\iscontainedin\Pic(S)\), of Enriques type: in the non-degenerate case \(h_\Co = F_1 + F_2\) with \(F_i^2 = 0\) and \(F_1\cdot F_2 = 1\), so that \(h_\Co^2 = 2\); its K3 pullback \(\tilde h_\Co\definedas f^{*}h_\Co\) lies in \(f^{*}(K_S^{\perp})\iscontainedin S_\Co\) and has \(\tilde h_\Co^2 = 4\).



Remark 30.10 (Why the two must not be identified) Both \(H\) and \(h_\Co\) have square \(2\) after pullback and square \(2\) downstairs respectively, so the numerical coincidence is easy to mistake for an identity. They are different classes: \(H\notin K_S^{\perp}\), since \(H\cdot K_S = -3\neq 0\), whereas \(h_\Co\) lies in \(K_S^{\perp}\) by definition, and their pullbacks have different squares, \(e_0^2 = 2\) against \(\tilde h_\Co^2 = 4\).
The analogue of the Enriques degree-\(2\) polarization is \(h_\Co\): polarization: for a degree-\(2\) Enriques surface the numerical polarization has \(h^2 = 2\) in \(\Num(Z)\cong E_{10}\) while the K3-side vector \(h = e + f\in U(2)\) has \(h^2 = 4\) (the discriminant description of \(\Gamma_{\En,2}\) (Proposition 42.7)), exactly the pattern of \(h_\Co\) and \(\tilde h_\Co\). Any comparison of Coble and Enriques polarized moduli, and any pairing of a polarization class against roots of a Coxeter diagram, must first record which of these classes is meant and in which lattice it lives.





Alexeev, Valery, Philip Engel, D. Zack Garza, and Luca Schaffler. 2025. “Compact Moduli of Enriques Surfaces with a Numerical Polarization of Degree 2.” Nagoya Mathematical Journal.


Cossec, François, Igor Dolgachev, and Christian Liedtke. 2025. Enriques Surfaces I. 2nd ed. Springer Nature Singapore. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-96-1214-7.

title: 33  Structure and classification facts for Coble surfaces
text:
34.1 Negative curves

Proposition 33.1 (Norms of smooth rational negative curves) Let \(S\) be a Coble surface with anti-bicanonical divisor \(D\). Every smooth rational negative curve \(E \iscontainedin S\) satisfies \[
E^2 \in \{-1,\, -2,\, -4\},
\] and if \(E^2 = -4\) then \(E\) is a component of \(D\).

This is the fact that makes the \((-4)\)-curves intrinsic: they cannot occur away from the boundary. It is the surface-level counterpart of the \(-2\) / \(-4\) norm dichotomy that governs the Coxeter diagrams in [[../computations/root-vectors-and-folded-sterk-diagrams.md]].
crumbs: 33  Structure and classification facts for Coble surfaces

title: 33  Structure and classification facts for Coble surfaces
text:
34.2 Automorphisms

Theorem 33.2 (Coble's theorem, lattice form) Write \(M_S \definedas K_S^{\perp\, \Pic(S)}\). Then \(\Aut(S)\) is isomorphic to a finite-index subgroup \(H \leq \Orth(M_S)\), and \[
\Orth(M_S)/\{\pm1\} \cong W(E_{10}).
\] For general \(C\), \(H \cong W(E_{10})(2)\), the level 2 congruence subgroup.

The project’s introduction records \(\Aut(S)\cong W(E_{10})\) for general \(C\); the refinement to the level 2 congruence subgroup, and the quotient statement for \(\Orth(M_S)\), are the sharper forms.

Remark 33.3 (Finiteness of negative curves modulo automorphisms) Let \(A_1(S)^{\mathrm{sm,rat},<0}\) denote the smooth rational curves of negative self-intersection. Then \(A_1(S)^{\mathrm{sm,rat},<0}/\Aut(S)\) is finite: up to automorphism a Coble surface carries only finitely many smooth rational negative curves. Classifying all surfaces with this property is an open question recorded in the source.
crumbs: 33  Structure and classification facts for Coble surfaces

title: 33  Structure and classification facts for Coble surfaces
text:
34.3 The Coble-Mukai lattice

Definition 33.4 (Coble-Mukai lattice) With \(B_1,\ldots,B_n\) the boundary components, set \[
L \definedas \generators{\NS(S),\ \tfrac12 B_1 + \cdots + \tfrac12 B_n}_\ZZ,
\qquad
\mathrm{CM}(S) \definedas \generators{B_1,\ldots,B_n}_\ZZ^{\perp L}.
\] \(\mathrm{CM}(S)\) serves as the replacement for \(\NS(S)\) in the Coble setting.

This object appears nowhere in the project, which works throughout with \(S_{\Co}\) and \(T_{\Co}\) inside \(\lkt\). Whether \(\mathrm{CM}(S)\) relates to \(S_{\Co}\), and whether it is the more natural home for the \(\Gamma_{\Co}\) action, is not addressed in the source and looks worth settling.

title: 33  Structure and classification facts for Coble surfaces
text:
34.4 The Dolgachev-Zhang classification

Definition 33.5 (Elliptic and rational types) A Coble surface is of elliptic type when there is \(S \birationaliso Y\) with \(|-K_Y|\) a singleton and the mobile part of \(|-2K_Y|\) generically a smooth elliptic curve. Elliptic type splits further:

Halphen type: blowups of singular points, and their infinitely near points, on a non-multiple fibre of a minimal rational elliptic surface with one multiple fibre of multiplicity 2.
Jacobian type: blowdowns of disjoint sections, and possibly components of one fibre, of a non-minimal rational elliptic surface with a section.

It is of rational type when the mobile part of \(|-2K_Y|\) consists of divisors \(D\) with \(p_a(D) = 0\), \(D\) not necessarily irreducible. These are blowups of minimal rational surfaces.


Theorem 33.6 (K3 type criterion, Dolgachev-Zhang Thm. 6.5) 
Let \(X\) be a Coble surface with \(M^2 = 0\).

If \(X\) is of Halphen type, obtained from a minimal Halphen surface \(Y_m\) of index 2 by one blowup of a singular point on its non-multiple fibre \(F\), then \(X\) is of K3 type if and only if \(F\) has type \(I_n\), \(\II\), \(\III\) or \(\IV\).
If \(X\) is of Jacobian type, obtained from a minimal Jacobian rational elliptic surface by blowing up a singular point of one fibre \(F\) and at least one singular point, with infinitely near points, on another fibre \(F_1\), then \(X\) is of K3 type if and only if each of \(F\) and \(F_1\) has type \(I_n\), \(\II\), \(\III\) or \(\IV\).



Lemma 33.7 (Dolgachev-Zhang Lem. 6.2) 
For a Coble surface \(X\) the following are equivalent:

\(|-2K_X|\) contains a reduced divisor;
there is a double cover \(\tilde X \to X\) with \(\tilde X\) a K3 surface having at worst ordinary double points.



Remark 33.8 (Why this matters for the Halphen program) The project’s Degenerations/Halphen_Surfaces.md records the Coble-to-Halphen blowdown and conjectures a correspondence of moduli spaces along the \(g=0\) line of Nikulin’s triangle; see [[../adjacent-programs/halphen-index-2-moduli-program.md]]. The elliptic/rational dichotomy and Theorem 6.5 are the classification that the conjecture must respect: they say exactly which Halphen and Jacobian configurations produce K3-type Cobles, and so which fibres of the conjectured correspondence are nonempty. The Jacobian branch has no counterpart anywhere in the project.

title: 33  Structure and classification facts for Coble surfaces
section: 34.5 Rational log Enriques surfaces of index 2
text:
34.5 Rational log Enriques surfaces of index 2

Definition 33.9 (Rational log Enriques surface of index 2) A normal rational surface \(\bar X\) with at worst quotient singularities such that \(\OO(-2K_{\bar X}) \cong \OO_{\bar X}\).


Theorem 33.10 (Terminal Cobles are resolutions of these) A terminal Coble surface is the minimal resolution of a maximum rational log Enriques surface of index 2. Conversely, the minimal resolution \(X\) of a rational log Enriques surface \(\bar X\) of index 2 is a Coble surface with \(h^0(-2K_X) = 1\), whose unique member \(D \in |-2K_X|\) is reduced and each of whose connected components is either a single \((-4)\)-curve or a linear chain with a prescribed dual graph.

The dual graph is a hand-drawn figure in the source and did not survive. If this characterization is used, that graph must be recovered from Dolgachev-Zhang.

title: 33  Structure and classification facts for Coble surfaces
section: 34.6 Dolgachev-Kondo geometry of the degree 2 polarization
text:
34.6 Dolgachev-Kondo geometry of the degree 2 polarization
The project’s Stable_Limits/Geometric.md records the map \(\phi_{ij}\) onto a quartic del Pezzo surface and the key fact that it is never finite in the Coble case. The following incidence data accompanying it is absent.

Remark 33.11 (The branch geometry) Take \(h = [F_1 + F_2] \in \Pic(S)\) of degree 2, so \(|h|\) defines \(\phi_{|h|}: S \to \PP^4\) with image \(D\) a 4-nodal quartic del Pezzo surface. Let \(\sigma\) be the deck transformation. Then:

\(\Fix(\sigma) = \bar W\) is a smooth genus 4 curve together with 3 isolated points;
\(\phi_h(C) = \{q\}\) is a singular point of \(D\), where \(C \in |-2K_S|\) is the Coble curve;
\(\bar W \intersect C = \{p_1, p_2\}\);
\(W \definedas \phi_h(\bar W)\) has \(p_a(W) = 5\) and a double point at \(q\).

A Coble surface arises as a degeneration of an Enriques surface exactly when the branch curve \(W\) passes through a singular point of \(D\).


Remark 33.12 (The rationality correspondence in its explicit form) Dolgachev-Kondo prove \(\fco\) rational by comparison with \(\mcm_{\mathrm{cusp}} = U/\PGL_3\), the moduli of cuspidal plane quintics. They show \(\mcm_{\mathrm{cusp}} \birationaliso \mcm_{\En}\), which is 10-dimensional, and that a distinguished codimension one locus \(\mcm'_{\mathrm{cusp}} \cong \mcm_{\Co}\). The locus is explicit: for \(C\) a plane quintic with cusp \(p\) and \(L\) the tangent line to \(C\) at \(p\), it is the case where \(L\) is also tangent to \(C\) at a smooth point \(q \in C\).
The project states only that \(\fco\) is rational “by relating it to a codimension one subvariety of a moduli space of certain \(A_2\)-singular quintics”. The tangency condition above is what cuts out that subvariety.

Related: [[coble-families-research-program.md]], [[../adjacent-programs/halphen-index-2-moduli-program.md]], [[cusp-correspondence-morphism-chain.md]].

title: 34  Rational Sextic Calculations
text: 34.1 The configuration constraint on the ten nodes

title: 34  Rational Sextic Calculations
text:
Proposition 34.5 (Ten nodes impose more conditions than the linear system has) The space of plane sextics is \[
\dim_\CC H^0\bigl(\PP^2, \OO_{\PP^2}(6)\bigr) = \binom{8}{2} = 28
,
\] so sextic curves form a \(\PP^{27}\). Requiring a singular point at a prescribed \(p\in\PP^2\) imposes three linear conditions on this space. Ten prescribed points therefore impose \(30\) conditions on a \(27\)-dimensional projective space, and for a general choice of \(p_1,\dots,p_{10}\) no sextic is singular at all ten. A sextic with ten nodes exists only when the ten points are special enough that the thirty conditions become dependent.


Proof. The monomials \(x^iy^jz^k\) with \(i+j+k=6\) number \(\binom{6+2}{2} = 28\), giving the stated dimension. For a fixed \(p\), singularity of \(\theset{F = 0}\) at \(p\) is the vanishing of the three partial derivatives \(\partial_x F(p)\), \(\partial_y F(p)\), \(\partial_z F(p)\); each is a linear condition on the coefficients of \(F\), and \(F(p) = 0\) follows from Euler’s identity \(\Sum_i x_i\,\partial_i F = 6F\). Imposing this at ten points gives \(30\) linear conditions on a space of projective dimension \(27\), so the general such linear system has empty intersection.


Remark 34.6 The dependence forced by Proposition 34.5 is what the term Coble point set names: a configuration \(\Sigma\) of ten points special enough to support a nodal sextic. The count is consistent with the moduli count in the GIT discussion of the Moduli Spaces section, where the configuration space \((\PP^2)^{10}/\PGL_3\) has dimension \(12\) and the Coble locus is cut out by three conditions, leaving the \(9\)-dimensional moduli of Corollary 47.5.


Remark 34.7 (How many of the thirty conditions are independent) Proposition 34.5 says the thirty conditions must be dependent but not by how much. The count is settled by the equisingular deformation theory of plane curves: for a curve of degree \(d\) with singularities whose root lattices are \(R_i\), the space of such curves has expected dimension \[
\binom{d+2}{2} - 1 - \Sum_i \rank(R_i)
,
\] and for sextics this expected dimension is attained (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 2.1). For ten nodes, \(\Sum_i\rank(R_i) = 10\), so the Severi variety \(V_{6,10}\) of Remark 34.2 has dimension \(27 - 10 = 17\): exactly ten of the thirty conditions are independent, one per node. Quotienting by the \(8\)-dimensional group \(\PGL_3\) leaves the nine moduli again.

title: 34  Rational Sextic Calculations
section: 34.2 A criterion for a node of a plane curve
text:
34.2 A criterion for a node of a plane curve

Proposition 34.8 (Hessian rank at a singular point) Let \(k\) be a field, let \(F\in k[x_0, x_1, x_2]\) be homogeneous of degree \(n\), and let \(p\in k^3\) be nonzero with \[
\partial_j F(p) = 0
\qquad\text{for } j = 0, 1, 2
.
\] Then the Hessian matrix \(H(F)(p) = \bigl(\partial_i\partial_j F(p)\bigr)_{ij}\) satisfies \(H(F)(p)\cdot p = 0\), and hence \[
\rank H(F)(p) \leq 2
.
\]


Proof. Euler’s identity for a homogeneous polynomial of degree \(n\) reads \(\Sum_i x_i\,\partial_i F = n F\). Differentiating it by \(\partial_j\) gives the polynomial identity \[
\Sum_i x_i\,\partial_j\partial_i F \;+\; \partial_j F \;=\; n\,\partial_j F
,
\] that is \(\Sum_i x_i\,\partial_i\partial_j F = (n-1)\,\partial_j F\). Evaluating at \(p\), where every first partial vanishes, gives \(H(F)(p)\cdot p = 0\). Since \(p\neq 0\) the kernel of \(H(F)(p)\) is nonzero, so by rank-nullity in dimension \(3\) the rank is at most \(2\).


Remark 34.9 Proposition 34.8 is the vanishing half of the node test for the sextic \(C\): at a singular point the Hessian is automatically degenerate, so the discriminating condition for an \(A_1\) singularity as opposed to a worse one is that the rank is exactly \(2\), the quadratic term of the local equation being then a nondegenerate binary quadratic form in the two directions transverse to \(p\). The statement holds over any field and for any degree, so it applies unchanged to the equations \(w^2 = F(x, y, z)\) of the K3 covers.

title: 35  Lattice Theory
text:
Remark 35.2 The study of semitoroidal compactifications of moduli spaces of Coble surfaces largely reduces to lattice theory, of which we will now recall the essential notions.


Remark 35.3 (Basic invariants) By a lattice, we mean a free \(\ZZ\)-module \(L\) of finite rank equipped with a nondegenerate1 symmetric integral bilinear form \(\beta_L: L \tensor_\ZZ L \to \ZZ\). We abbreviate \(vw \definedas \beta_L(v, w)\) and \(v^2 \definedas \beta_L(v, v)\) and refer to the latter as the norm of \(v\). We write \(L_R \definedas L\tensor_{\ZZ} R\) and \(\beta_{L_R}\) for \(R = \QQ, \RR, \CC\) for the \(\ZZ\)-linear extensions of \((L, \beta_L)\) to the rational, real, and complex numbers respectively.
A submodule \(M\iscontainedin L\) is a sublattice if the restricted bilinear form \(\restrictionof{\beta_L}{M}\) endows \(M\) with the structure of a lattice. A vector \(v\in L\) is isotropic if \(v^2 = 0\), i.e. it is norm zero, and more generally a sublattice \(M \iscontainedin L\) is isotropic if \(\restrictionof{\beta_L}{M} \equiv 0\). A lattice is said to be even if \(x^2\in 2\ZZ\) for all \(x\in L\), and odd otherwise. A nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form can be linearly extended to \(L_\RR\) and by Sylvester’s theorem, diagonalized with only \(1\) or \(-1\) on the diagonal. We write \(n_+\) and \(n_-\) respectively for the number of \(\pm 1\) entries on the diagonal. The signature of \(L\) is the pair \((n_+, n_-)\), and the index is \(n_+ - n_-\). We say \(L\) is definite if either \(n_+\) or \(n_-\) is zero, and indefinite otherwise. More precisely, if \(n_- = 0\) we say \(L\) is positive definite, and similarly if \(n_+ = 0\), we say \(L\) is negative definite. A negative definite lattice generated by elements of norm \(-2\) is said to be a root lattice, and such elements are referred to as roots.
The rank \(r\) of a lattice is its rank as a free \(\ZZ\)-module and is given by \(r=n_+ + n_- = \dim_\QQ L_\QQ\). An indefinite lattice of signature \((1, r-1)\) is said to be hyperbolic. Fixing a generating set \(e_i\) of \(L\), we define the Gram matrix of \(L\) as the matrix \(G_L \definedas (\beta_L(e_i, e_j))_{ij}\), and the discriminant as \(\operatorname{disc} L \definedas \det G_L\). The discriminant is independent of the choice of generating set.


Remark 35.4 (Finiteness in the definite and indefinite cases) Write \(L[k] \definedas \theset{v\in L \mid v^2 = k}\) for the set of vectors of norm \(k\).
If \(L\) is definite then \(L[k]\) is finite for every \(k\), since the real extension of \(\pm\beta_L\) is a positive definite quadratic form on \(L_\RR\) and \(L\) is discrete, so a bounded region contains finitely many lattice points. For the same reason \(\Orth(L)\) is finite: an isometry is determined by the images of a basis \(e_1,\dots,e_r\), and it carries \(e_i\) into the finite set \(L[e_i^2]\).
Neither statement survives indefiniteness. In \(U = \ZZ e\oplus\ZZ f\) one has \(U[0] = \ZZ e\union\ZZ f\), which is infinite. In \(L = \generators{1}\oplus\generators{-2}\) the set \(L[1]\) is the solution set of the Pell equation \(x^2 - 2y^2 = 1\), again infinite, and \[
M = \begin{bmatrix}3&4\\2&3\end{bmatrix}
\qquad\text{satisfies}\qquad
M^{\mathsf T} G_L M = G_L,
\qquad G_L = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-2\end{bmatrix}
,
\] with \(M\) of infinite order, so \(\Orth(L)\) is infinite. Enumerating a level set or an orthogonal group is therefore not by itself an available operation for the hyperbolic lattices of this monograph, and the reflection groups of the Compactifications sections are described instead by a fundamental chamber with finitely many walls.


Remark 35.5 (Discriminant forms) The dual lattice to \(L\) is denoted \(\dualof{L} \definedas \Hom_\ZZ(L, \ZZ)\), and there is an morphism \[
\begin{aligned}
\iota: L &\injects \dualof{L} \\
x &\mapsto \beta_L(x, \cdot)
\end{aligned}
\] which, if \(L\) is nondegenerate, is an injection with finite index image. The discriminant group is \(A_L \definedas \coker \iota \cong \dualof{L}/L\); this is a finite order group of order \(\abs{\operatorname{disc} L}\). We say \(L\) is unimodular if any of the following equivalent conditions hold:

\(A_L\) is the trivial group,
\(\iota\) is an isomorphism and \(L\cong \dualof{L}\),
\(\abs{ \operatorname{disc} L} = 1\).

If \(A_L \cong (\zpz)^a\) for some \(a\), we say \(L\) is \(p\)-elementary; in our applications we will often have \(p=2\). For even lattices, the form \(\beta_L\) descends to a well-defined quadratic form \[
\begin{aligned}
q_L: A_L &\to \QQ/2\ZZ \\
x + L &\mapsto \beta_{L_\QQ}(x, x) \mod 2\ZZ
\end{aligned}
\] We call the pair \((A_L, q_L)\) the discriminant quadratic form of \(L\). A morphism between two lattices is a morphism of \(\ZZ\)-modules \(\eta: L\to L'\) respecting the bilinear forms in the sense that \(\beta_L(x, y) = \beta_{L'}(\eta(x), \eta(y))\), and is a primitive embedding if \(\eta\) is injective and \(\coker \eta\) is torsionfree. An isometry of lattices is an isomorphism, defined in the obvious way. We write \(\Orth(L)\) for the group of lattice automorphisms of \(L\), denoted the orthogonal group of \(L\), and similarly \(\Orth(q_L)\) for the \(\ZZ\)-module automorphisms of the discriminant group \(A_L\) which preserve the quadratic form. There is a natural group homomorphism \(\Orth(L)\to\Orth(q_L)\), the kernel is denoted \(\tilde \Orth(L)\), equivalently written \(\Orth(L)^*\); we call it the stable orthogonal group. When \(L\) has signature \((2, n)\), the associated period domain \(\Omega_L\) has two connected components interchanged by complex conjugation, and we write \(\Orth^+(L)\) for the index-two subgroup of \(\Orth(L)\) preserving each component (equivalently, preserving the orientation of the positive-definite part, i.e. those isometries of real spinor norm \(+1\)). We write \(\Orth^+(L)^* \definedas \Orth^+(L)\intersect \tilde\Orth(L)\) for the intersection, which is the arithmetic group acting on a single component \(D_L\).


Definition 35.6 (Marked hyperkähler moduli, periods, and monodromy) Fix a deformation type \(\mathscr D\) of compact irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifolds and an abstract lattice \(\Lambda\) such that for every \(X\in\mathscr D\) there is an isometry \[
\qty{H^2(X,\ZZ),q_X}\iso\Lambda,
\] where \(q_X\) is the Beauville–Bogomolov form.
A \(\Lambda\)-marking of \(X\) is an isometry of lattices \[
\eta\colon\qty{H^2(X,\ZZ),q_X}\iso\Lambda.
\] A \(\Lambda\)-marked pair is a pair \((X,\eta)\) with \(X\in\mathscr D\) and \(\eta\) a \(\Lambda\)-marking. Two marked pairs \((X,\eta)\) and \((X',\eta')\) are isomorphic if there exists a biholomorphism \(f\colon X\iso X'\) such that \[
\eta'=\eta\circ f^*\colon H^2(X',\ZZ)\too\Lambda.
\] The marked moduli space is \[
\mathcal M_{\mathrm{marked}}
=\mathcal M_{\mathrm{marked}}(\mathscr D,\Lambda)
\definedas
\theset{\text{$\Lambda$-marked pairs $(X,\eta)$ of type $\mathscr D$}}/\cong.
\] A symbol \[
\mathcal M^0_{\mathrm{marked}}\in\pi_0\qty{\mathcal M_{\mathrm{marked}}}
\] means a fixed connected component of this marked moduli space.
For a marking \(\eta\), write \[
\eta_\RR\definedas\eta\tensor_\ZZ\RR,
\qquad
\eta_\CC\definedas\eta\tensor_\ZZ\CC.
\] When no ambiguity is possible, \(\eta(H)\) for \(H\in H^2(X,\RR)\) means \(\eta_\RR(H)\).
The marked period domain is \[
\Omega_{\mathrm{marked}}
\definedas
\theset{[x]\in\PP(\Lambda_\CC)\st (x,x)=0,\ (x,\bar x)>0}.
\] The period map is \[
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{marked}}\colon
\mathcal M_{\mathrm{marked}}\too\Omega_{\mathrm{marked}},
\qquad
(X,\eta)\longmapsto\eta_\CC\qty{H^{2,0}(X)}.
\] Its restriction to \(\mathcal M^0_{\mathrm{marked}}\) is denoted \[
\mathcal P^0_{\mathrm{marked}}
\definedas
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{marked}}\vert_{\mathcal M^0_{\mathrm{marked}}}.
\] Thus \((X,\eta)\) has period \([x]\) precisely when \[
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{marked}}(X,\eta)=[x]
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\CC x=\eta_\CC\qty{H^{2,0}(X)}.
\]
Let \(X,X'\in\mathscr D\). A parallel-transport operator \[
T\colon H^2(X,\ZZ)\iso H^2(X',\ZZ)
\] is an isomorphism induced by parallel transport in the local system \(R^2\pi_*\ZZ\) along a path between fibers isomorphic to \(X\) and \(X'\) in a smooth proper family \(\pi\colon\mathcal X\to B\) of manifolds of type \(\mathscr D\). If \(X'=X\), \(T\) is a monodromy operator. The degree-two monodromy group is \[
\operatorname{Mon}(X)
\definedas
\theset{T\in\Orth\qty{H^2(X,\ZZ),q_X}\st T\text{ is a monodromy operator}}.
\] For \((X,\eta)\in\mathcal M^0_{\mathrm{marked}}\), define \[
\operatorname{Mon}\qty{\mathcal M^0_{\mathrm{marked}}}
\definedas
\eta\,\operatorname{Mon}(X)\,\eta^{-1}
\iscontainedin\Orth(\Lambda).
\] This subgroup is independent of the chosen \((X,\eta)\) inside the fixed component: if \((X,\eta)\) and \((X',\eta')\) lie in the same component, then \(\eta'^{-1}\eta\colon H^2(X,\ZZ)\iso H^2(X',\ZZ)\) is a parallel-transport operator and conjugates the two fiberwise monodromy groups. Different components give conjugate subgroups of \(\Orth(\Lambda)\). If these conjugate subgroups coincide—for example under the normality hypothesis on \(\operatorname{Mon}(X)\) used by Song—their common value is denoted \[
\operatorname{Mon}(\Lambda)\iscontainedin\Orth(\Lambda).
\]


Definition 35.7 (The spinor norm and the special orthogonal group) Every \(g\in\Orth(L_\RR)\) is a product of reflections \(g = s_{w_1}\cdots s_{w_m}\) in anisotropic vectors \(w_i\), where \(s_w(x) = x - 2\tfrac{\beta(x, w)}{\beta(w,w)}w\). The real spinor norm of \(g\) is \[
\spinornorm_\RR(g) \definedas \prod_{i=1}^{m} \frac{-\beta(w_i, w_i)}{2}
\ \in\ \unitsof{\RR}/(\unitsof{\RR})^2
,
\] which is independent of the chosen decomposition. The subgroup \(\Orth^+(L_\RR)\) is the kernel of \(\spinornorm_\RR\), and for a hyperbolic lattice it is the index-two subgroup preserving the positive cone. The special orthogonal group is the index-two subgroup \[
\SO(L) \definedas \ker\bigl(\det\colon \Orth(L)\to\theset{\pm 1}\bigr)
,
\] and we write \(\SO^+(L)\definedas\Orth^+(L)\intersect\SO(L)\) and \(\widetilde{\SO}^+(L)\definedas\Orth^+(L)\intersect\tilde\Orth(L)\intersect\SO(L)\).


Definition 35.8 (The positive-cone orientation character) Let \(\Lambda\) be a lattice of signature \((3,b_2-3)\) and set \[
\widetilde C_\Lambda \definedas \theset{x\in\Lambda_\RR \st (x,x)>0}.
\] For any positive-definite three-plane \(W_3\containedin\Lambda_\RR\), the inclusion \[
W_3\sm\theset{0}\ \injects\ \widetilde C_\Lambda
\] is a homotopy equivalence: after an orthogonal decomposition \(\Lambda_\RR=W_3\oplus W_3^\perp\), scaling the \(W_3^\perp\)-component to zero preserves the inequality \((x,x)>0\). Hence \[
H_2\qty{W_3\sm\theset{0},\ZZ}\iso H_2\qty{\widetilde C_\Lambda,\ZZ}\iso\ZZ.
\] An orientation of \(W_3\) determines one of the two generators of this group; these two generators are the orientation classes of \(\widetilde C_\Lambda\). The action of \(\Orth(\Lambda_\RR)\) on these two classes defines a character \[
\sigma_+\colon \Orth(\Lambda_\RR)\too\theset{\pm1}.
\] With the real-spinor-norm convention above, \(\sigma_+\) is the spinor-norm character. For \(G\leq\Orth(\Lambda)\) write \[
G^+\definedas\ker\qty{\sigma_+\vert_G}.
\] This is the orientation-class formulation of the spinor character used in E. Markman, A survey of Torelli and monodromy results for holomorphic-symplectic varieties, §4 (2011, arXiv:1101.4606).


Proposition 35.9 (Hyperkähler monodromy has trivial spinor norm) Let \(\mathcal M^0_{\mathrm{marked}}\) be a connected component of the moduli space of marked compact hyperkähler manifolds with marking \[
\eta\colon H^2(X,\ZZ)\iso\Lambda.
\] Then its monodromy group satisfies \[
\operatorname{Mon}\qty{\mathcal M^0_{\mathrm{marked}}}\ \iscontainedin\ \Orth^+(\Lambda)\definedas\ker\sigma_+.
\] In particular, whenever the monodromy groups of the fibers are identified with a subgroup \(\operatorname{Mon}(\Lambda)\leq\Orth(\Lambda)\) independent of the chosen marked component, one has \[
\operatorname{Mon}(\Lambda)\iscontainedin\Orth^+(\Lambda).
\]


Proof. Let \((X,\eta)\in\mathcal M^0_{\mathrm{marked}}\) have period \([x]\), and choose a Kähler class \(H\in H^{1,1}(X,\RR)\). The real three-plane \[
W_{X,H}\definedas \CC x\oplus\RR\eta(H)
=\Span_\RR\qty{\Re x,\Im x,\eta(H)}
\containedin\Lambda_\RR
\] is positive definite, and the ordered basis \[
\qty{\Re x,\Im x,\eta(H)}
\] determines an orientation class of \(\widetilde C_\Lambda\). As \((X,\eta,H)\) varies continuously, this class is locally constant and hence constant on the connected component \(\mathcal M^0_{\mathrm{marked}}\). A monodromy operator is induced by parallel transport around a loop in this component, so it preserves the distinguished orientation class. Therefore its image under \(\sigma_+\) is \(+1\), proving the containment.


Remark 35.10 (Relation with the period-domain convention) For hyperkähler \(H^2\), the Beauville–Bogomolov lattice has signature \((3,b_2-3)\), so \(\Orth^+(\Lambda)\) is naturally described by preservation of an orientation class of a positive three-plane. After fixing a positive class \(h\) and passing to \(h^\perp\) of signature \((2,b_2-3)\), the same orientation data becomes the usual choice of connected component of the type-IV period domain.


Remark 35.11 (Orthogonal complements) Given two lattices \(L_1, L_2\) we write \(L_1\oplus L_2\) for the orthogonal direct sum, which is the direct sum of the underlying modules with bilinear form defined by \[
\beta_{L_1\oplus L_2}(v_1 + v_2, w_1 + w_2)\definedas \beta_{L_1}(v_1, w_1) + \beta_{L_2}(v_2, w_2)
.
\] We write \(L^{\oplus n}\) for the direct sum of \(n\) copies of \(L\). Let \(\eta: M \injects L\) be a primitive embedding of lattices, for example the inclusion of a sublattice. We write \[
M^{\perp L} \definedas \theset{x\in L \mid \beta_L(x, M) = 0}
.
\] If the ambient lattice \(L\) is understood, we often abuse notation and simply write \(M^{\perp}\) without reference to \(L\). Note that \(M^{\perp L}\oplus M \iscontainedin L\) may not be saturated, and is generally a finite index sublattice of \(L\). We note that \(M^{\perp L}\intersect M \neq \theset{0}\) in general.2 We also note that for any lattices \(L_i\), \[
A_{L_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus L_n} = A_{L_1} \oplus \cdots \oplus A_{L_n}
\]


Remark 35.12 (2-elementary lattices) Let \(L\) be a 2-elementary lattice. The divisibility of a vector \(v\in L\), denoted \(\operatorname{div}_L(v)\), is defined by \(\beta_L(v, L) = \operatorname{div}_L(v)\ZZ\), i.e. the positive integral generator of the image of the map \(\beta_L(v, \cdot): L\to \ZZ\). For 2-elementary lattices, one always has \(\operatorname{div}_L(v) \in \theset{1, 2}\). We set \(v^* \definedas v/\operatorname{div}_L(v)\in A_L\). Letting \(q_L:A_L \to {1\over 2}\ZZ/\ZZ\) be the induced quadratic form on \(A_L\), we say \(v^*\) is characteristic if \(q_L(x) = \beta_L(v^*, x)\mod \ZZ\) for all \(x\in A_L\), and is ordinary otherwise. We say that a primitive isotropic vector \(e\in L\) is

odd if \(\operatorname{div}_L(e) = 1\),
even ordinary if \(\operatorname{div}_L(e) = 2\) and \(e^*\) is ordinary, or
even characteristic if \(\operatorname{div}_L(e) = 2\) and \(e^*\) is characteristic.

The 2-elementary hyperbolic lattices admitting a primitive embedding into \(\lkt\) were classified by Nikulin in (Nikulin 1980, sec. 3.6.2). An indefinite even 2-elementary lattice is determined up to isometry by its signature together with a triple of invariants \((r,a,\delta)\). Here, \(r\definedas \rank_\ZZ(L)\) is the rank, \(a = \rank_{\bF_2}A_L\) is the exponent appearing in \(A_L = (\ZZ/2\ZZ)^a\), and \(\delta \in \theset{0, 1}\) is the coparity: we set \(\delta = 0\) if \(q_L(A_L) \iscontainedin \ZZ\), so \(q_L(x) \equiv 0 \mod \ZZ\) for all \(x\in A_L\), and \(\delta=1\) otherwise. The evenness and indefiniteness hypotheses are both needed: the theorem is Nikulin’s classification of even 2-elementary lattices, and it rests on the general uniqueness criterion for even indefinite lattices (Nikulin 1980 Thm. 1.14.2). We accordingly specify such lattices using the notation \((r,a,\delta)_{n_+}\).


Theorem 35.13 (Classification of primitive isotropic vectors by type) Let \(S\) be an even hyperbolic 2-elementary lattice with invariants \((r, a, \delta)\), let \(v\in S\) be a primitive isotropic vector, and write \(\oS\definedas v^{\perp S}/v\). Then exactly one of the following holds, according to the type of \(v\) in the sense above, and in each case \(S\) splits off the indicated rank-two summand containing \(v\):

odd: \(S \cong U\oplus\oS\), with \(a_{\oS} = a\) and \(\delta_{\oS} = \delta\);
even ordinary: \(S \cong U(2)\oplus\oS\), with \(a_{\oS} = a - 2\) and \(\delta_{\oS} = \delta\);
even characteristic: \(S \cong \latI_{1,1}(2)\oplus\oS\), with \(a_{\oS} = a - 2\); this case forces \(\delta = 1\) and gives \(\delta_{\oS} = 0\).

In all three cases \(\oS\) is even negative definite of rank \(r - 2\). Classifying the primitive isotropic vectors of \(S\) up to isometry is therefore equivalent to classifying the even negative definite lattices with invariants \((r-2, a, \delta)\), \((r-2, a-2, \delta)\) and \((r-2, a-2, 0)\).


Proof. This is (Alexeev and Engel 2022 Prop. 5.5).


Remark 35.14 The isotropic-trichotomy theorem (Theorem 35.13) is the tool by which a \(0\)-cusp of a type IV quotient is identified from a single numerical invariant of its isotropic vector: the divisibility, together with the characteristic-or-ordinary dichotomy, determines the invariants of the boundary lattice \(\overline{S}\), and for indefinite \(\overline{S}\) those invariants determine its isometry class. It is used in this form throughout the cusp correspondence.


Remark 35.15 (Twists of a lattice) If \(L\) is a lattice with bilinear form \(\beta_L\), define \(L(n)\) to be the twist of \(L\) by \(n\), which has the same underlying \(\ZZ\)-module but is equipped with the scaled bilinear form \[
\beta_{L(n)}(v,w) \definedas n\cdot \beta_L(v, w).
\]


Remark 35.16 (The lattice $\generators{n}$) The lattice \(\generators{n}\) is defined as the rank 1 lattice \(\ZZ\) with one generator \(v\) satisfying \(\beta_{\generators{n}}(v,v) = n\). The Gram matrix is the \(1\times 1\) matrix \(G_{\generators n} = [n]\), and the associated quadratic form is \(q_{\generators{n}}(x) = nx^2\).


Remark 35.17 (The hyperbolic lattice) In rank 2, there are two unimodular hyperbolic lattices: the odd \(\latI_{1, 1} \definedas \generators{1} \oplus \generators{-1}\), and the even \(U\definedas \latII_{1, 1}\). We refer to the latter as the hyperbolic lattice, which can be realized as \(U \definedas \ZZ e \oplus \ZZ f\) with \(e^2=f^2 = 0\) and \(ef = 1\), and thus the following Gram matrix: \[
G_U = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}
.
\]


Remark 35.18 (ADE lattices) 
Any Dynkin diagram of type \(A_n, D_n, E_6, E_7, E_8\) corresponds to a root lattice of the respective type. By convention, we take the negative definite twists of these lattices. Of particular importance to us is the \(E_8\) lattice associated to the following Dynkin diagram:
















































































Figure 35.1: The Dynkin diagram \(E_{8}\).





Remark 35.19 (The lattice $\latI_{p, q}$) For any pair of non-negative integers \((p, q)\), there exists an odd indefinite unimodular lattice determined up to isomorphism by its rank and signature: \[
\latI_{p, q} \definedas \generators{1}^{\oplus p}\oplus \generators{-1}^{\oplus q}
.
\]


Remark 35.20 (The lattice $\latII_{p, q}$) Let \(L\) be an even indefinite unimodular lattice of signature \((p, q)\). Then \(p-q\equiv 0 \pmod 8\), and \(L\) is uniquely determined up to isomorphism by its rank and signature: \[
\latII_{p, q} \definedas
\begin{cases}
    U ^{\oplus p}\oplus E_8^{\oplus {q-p\over 8}}, & p < q \\
    U^{\oplus q} \oplus E_8(-1)^{\oplus {p-q\over 8}}, & p > q
.\end{cases}
\]

title: 36  Root systems and root lattices
text:
Definition 36.2 Let \(L\) be a lattice (in the Euclidean model, positive definite). The set of roots of \(L\) is \[
R(L) \definedas \theset{ v\in L \mid v^2 = 2 }
.
\] A simple root system \(\Phi(L)\iscontainedin R(L)\) is a subset of roots \(\theset{\alpha_i}\) such that every root \(v\in R(L)\) is either a nonnegative integer combination or a nonpositive integer combination of the \(\alpha_i\) — the positive and negative roots respectively; that is, \[
R(L) = \ZZ_{\geq 0}\,\Phi(L) \;\sqcup\; \ZZ_{\leq 0}\,\Phi(L)
,
\] so every \(v\in R(L)\) can be written as \(v = \Sum_{\alpha_i\in \Phi(L)} c_i \alpha_i\) with all \(c_i\in \ZZ_{\geq 0}\) or all \(c_i\in \ZZ_{\leq 0}\). The elements of \(\Phi(L)\) are the simple roots. Any simple root system spans a sublattice \(\ZZ\Phi(L)\injects L\), and we say \(L\) is a root lattice if this inclusion has index \(1\), i.e. \(L = \ZZ\Phi(L)\).


Remark 36.3 (The Weyl group) For a root \(\alpha\in R(L)\), the associated reflection is the isometry \[
\begin{aligned}
s_\alpha: L_\QQ &\to L_\QQ \\
x &\mapsto x - \frac{2\,\beta_L(x,\alpha)}{\beta_L(\alpha,\alpha)}\,\alpha
= x - \beta_L(x,\alpha)\,\alpha
,
\end{aligned}
\] the second equality holding because \(\alpha^2 = 2\). It fixes the hyperplane \(H_\alpha \definedas \alpha^{\perp L}\) pointwise and sends \(\alpha\mapsto -\alpha\). The Weyl group of \(L\) is the subgroup \[
W(L) \definedas \generators{\, s_{\alpha_i} \mid \alpha_i\in \Phi(L) \,} \leq \Orth(L)
\] generated by the reflections in the simple roots.
For a root lattice we may identify the Gram matrix \(G_L\) with \(G_{\ZZ\Phi(L)}\), the matrix of pairings \(\beta_L(\alpha_i,\alpha_j)\) between the simple roots; its diagonal entries are \(\alpha_i^2 = 2\) and its off-diagonal entries record the intersections of simple roots.

title: 36  Root systems and root lattices
text:
36.2 The \(ADE\) lattices
The simply-laced root lattices \(A_n\), \(D_n\), \(E_n\) have a single root length and are the ones that occur in the lattice theory of \(K3\) and Coble surfaces.

Definition 36.4 Let \(\ZZ^{n+1}\) denote the standard diagonal lattice \(\generators{1}^{\oplus (n+1)}\) with orthonormal generators \(\theset{e_1,\dots,e_{n+1}}\), and set \(v_{n+1} \definedas \Sum_{i=1}^{n+1} e_i\). The root lattice \(A_n\) is realized as the primitive sublattice \[
A_n \cong v_{n+1}^{\perp\, \ZZ^{n+1}}
= \theset{ x\in \ZZ^{n+1} \mid \textstyle\Sum_{i=1}^{n+1} x_i = 0 }
.
\] Its roots are the difference vectors \[
R(A_n) = \theset{ r_{ij} \definedas e_i - e_j \mid 1\leq i\neq j\leq n+1 }
,
\] of which there are \(n(n+1)\). A simple system is given by the \(n\) vectors \[
\alpha_i \definedas e_i - e_{i+1},
\qquad 1\leq i\leq n
.
\]


Definition 36.5 The root lattice \(D_n\) is the sublattice of \(\ZZ^n\) cut out by the even-coordinate-sum condition, i.e. the kernel of the reduction \(\varepsilon_2: \ZZ^n \to \ZZ/2\ZZ\), \(x\mapsto \Sum_i x_i \bmod 2\): \[
D_n \cong \ZZ^n_{\mathrm{ev}}
\definedas \theset{ x = (x_1,\dots,x_n)\in \ZZ^n \mid \textstyle\Sum_{i=1}^n x_i \equiv 0 \pmod{2} }
\injects \ZZ^n
.
\] Its roots are \[
R(D_n) = \theset{ \pm e_i \pm e_j \mid 1\leq i < j\leq n }
,
\] of which there are \(2n(n-1)\). A simple system is given by \[
\alpha_i \definedas e_i - e_{i+1} \ \ (1\leq i\leq n-1),
\qquad
\alpha_n \definedas e_{n-1} + e_n
.
\]


Definition 36.6 The root lattice \(E_8\) is realized inside \(\QQ^8\) as \[
E_8 \cong \theset{ x\in \ZZ^8 \union (\ZZ^8 + \tfrac12 v_8) \mid
\textstyle\Sum_{i=1}^8 x_i \equiv 0 \pmod 2 },
\qquad v_8 = (1,\dots,1)
,
\] so that \(E_8\) consists of all integer vectors and all half-integer vectors whose coordinate sum is even. The lattices \(E_7\) and \(E_6\) are obtained as orthogonal complements inside \(E_8\): \[
E_7 \definedas L_1^{\perp\, E_8}
\quad\text{for any } L_1\leq E_8 \text{ isometric to } A_1,
\qquad
E_6 \definedas L_2^{\perp\, E_8}
\quad\text{for any } L_2\leq E_8 \text{ isometric to } A_2
.
\] (Here \(A_1 = \generators{2}\) is generated by a single root and \(A_2\) by two roots meeting at the usual angle; the isometry type of the complement is independent of the chosen sublattice.)


Example 36.7 The lattice \(E_8\) contains exactly \[
2^4\cdot 3\cdot 5 = 240
\] roots, of two kinds:

the \(112\) difference vectors \(\pm e_i \pm e_j\) for \(1\leq i < j\leq 8\) (these are the roots of the \(D_8\) sublattice), and
the \(128\) half-sum vectors \(\tfrac12(\pm e_1 \pm \cdots \pm e_8)\) with an even number of minus signs.

Indeed \(\binom{8}{2}\cdot 4 = 112\) and \(2^{8-1} = 128\), giving \(240\) in total. There are \(8\) simple roots comprising \(\Phi(E_8)\), and the Weyl group \(W(E_8)\) acts transitively on the root set \(R(E_8)\).


Theorem 36.8 \(E_8\) is the unique even, unimodular, positive-definite lattice of rank \(8\). In particular it is self-dual, \(E_8 \cong \dualof{E_8}\).


Remark 36.9 The characterization in the \(E_8\) characterization theorem (Theorem 36.8) is a classical fact of lattice theory (Conway and Sloane 2010). The construction of the \(E_n\) lattice definition (Definition 36.6) exhibits \(E_8\) concretely as the overlattice \(D_8^+\) of \(D_8\) (see the plus-construction definition (Definition 36.13) and the plus-construction theorem (Theorem 36.14)), which makes both the evenness and the unimodularity transparent.

title: 36  Root systems and root lattices
text:
36.3 Non-simply-laced root systems
The following root systems carry two root lengths and so are not root lattices in the sense of the root-lattice definition (Definition 36.2); we record them for completeness in the Euclidean model.

Remark 36.10 (Which reflection groups arise from a lattice) The systems recorded in this section are exactly the crystallographic ones (Definition 50.22), those with all \(m_{ij}\in\theset{2,3,4,6}\). The remaining finite reflection groups \(H_3\), \(H_4\) and \(I_2(p)\) for \(p\notin\theset{2,3,4,6}\) preserve no lattice of full rank (Theorem 50.23), and so are finite Coxeter systems that are the Weyl group of no root system in a lattice; their Gram forms are defined over the real number fields of Example 50.28 rather than over \(\ZZ\).


Definition 36.11 The root system \(R(B_n)\iscontainedin \ZZ^n\) consists of the short roots \(r_i \definedas \pm e_i\) for \(1\leq i\leq n\) together with the long roots \(r_{ij} \definedas \pm e_i \pm e_j\) for \(1\leq i < j\leq n\); there are \(2n + 2n(n-1) = 2n^2\) roots in total (\(2n\) short, \(2n(n-1)\) long). A simple system is \[
\alpha_i \definedas e_i - e_{i+1} \ \ (1\leq i\leq n-1),
\qquad \alpha_n \definedas e_n
.
\]
The root system \(R(C_n)\) is dual to \(B_n\): it consists of the long roots \(2r_i = \pm 2e_i\) together with the short roots \(r_{ij} = \pm e_i \pm e_j\), again \(2n^2\) roots in total (\(2n\) long, \(2n(n-1)\) short). A simple system is \[
\alpha_i \definedas e_i - e_{i+1} \ \ (1\leq i\leq n-1),
\qquad \alpha_n \definedas 2e_n
.
\]


Definition 36.12 The root system \(F_4\) is realized in \(\ZZ^4\) with root set \(R(F_4)\) comprising the \(24\) long roots \(\pm e_i \pm e_j\) for \(1\leq i < j\leq 4\) together with the \(24\) short roots consisting of the \(8\) vectors \(\pm e_i\) (\(1\leq i\leq 4\)) and the \(16\) half-sums \(\tfrac12(\pm e_1 \pm e_2 \pm e_3 \pm e_4)\) ranging over all \(2^4\) sign patterns, giving \(48\) roots in all. A system of simple roots is \[
\alpha_1 = e_2 - e_3,\quad
\alpha_2 = e_3 - e_4,\quad
\alpha_3 = e_4,\quad
\alpha_4 = \tfrac12(e_1 - e_2 - e_3 - e_4)
.
\]
The root system \(G_2\) embeds into the trace-zero sublattice \(\ZZ^3_\Delta \definedas \theset{ x\in \ZZ^3 \mid \Sum_i x_i = 0 } \iscontainedin \ZZ^3\). Its roots are the vectors \(\pm(e_i - e_j)\) and \(\pm(2e_i - e_j - e_k)\), twelve in total. A simple system is \[
\alpha_1 = e_1 - e_2,
\qquad
\alpha_2 = -e_1 + 2e_2 - e_3
.
\]

title: 36  Root systems and root lattices
text:
36.4 The plus construction and \(D_8^+ \cong E_8\)
The realization of \(E_8\) in the \(E_n\) lattice definition (Definition 36.6) is an instance of a general overlattice construction for the \(D_n\) family.

Definition 36.13 Define two vectors in \(\QQ^n\) by \[
v_+ = \tfrac12(1,1,1,\dots,1),
\qquad
v_- = \tfrac12(-1,1,1,\dots,1)
.
\] The plus and minus overlattices of \(D_n\) are \[
D_n^+ \definedas D_n \union (v_+ + D_n),
\qquad
D_n^- \definedas D_n \union (v_- + D_n)
,
\] each obtained by adjoining one half-integer coset to \(D_n\).


Theorem 36.14 
Let \(D_n^+ = D_n\union(v_+ + D_n)\) with \(v_+ = \tfrac12(1,\dots,1)\) be the overlattice of the plus-construction definition (Definition 36.13).

\(D_n^+\) is a lattice if and only if \(n\) is even. For \(n\) odd, \(2v_+ = (1,\dots,1)\notin D_n\) — equivalently \([v_+]\) has order \(4\) in \(A_{D_n}\cong\ZZ/4\ZZ\) — so the coset union is not closed under addition and is not a lattice.
For \(n\) even, \(D_n^+\) contains \(D_n\) as a sublattice of index \(2\) and has determinant \(1\).
\(D_n^+\) is an integral lattice (hence unimodular) if and only if \(4\mid n\), and is even if and only if \(8\mid n\). For \(n\equiv 2\pmod 4\) the lattice \(D_n^+\) has determinant \(1\) but is non-integral, since \(v_+^2 = n/4\notin\ZZ\).
In particular \(D_8^+ \cong E_8\) is the even unimodular lattice of rank \(8\).



Remark 36.15 The properties in the plus-construction theorem (Theorem 36.14) are standard for the \(D_n\) family (Conway and Sloane 2010). Because \(D_8^+\) is unimodular and contains \(D_8\) with index \(2\), the even-coordinate-sum sublattice \(D_8\) has discriminant group of order \(4\); the half-integer coset \(v_+ + D_8\) supplies precisely the \(128\) half-sum roots of \(E_8\) recorded in the \(E_8\) root example (Example 36.7), while the \(112\) roots of \(D_8\) supply the difference vectors. This recovers the count \(112 + 128 = 240\) and identifies \(E_8\) with \(D_8^+\).

title: 36  Root systems and root lattices
section: 36.5 Root lattices of the two-elementary reflection groups
text:
36.5 Root lattices of the two-elementary reflection groups

Proposition 36.16 (\(B_n(2)\), \(C_n\) and \(F_4\) in the two-elementary setting) An even \(2\)-elementary lattice has roots of two norms, the short roots \(v^2 = -2\) and the long roots \(v^2 = -4\) of divisibility \(2\) (Definition 49.4), so its reflection group can have a non-simply-laced Coxeter diagram. The three families that occur are \(B_n(2)\), \(C_n\) and \(F_4\), and as lattices generated by their short roots alone they are \[
B_n(2) = A_1^{\oplus n},
\qquad
C_n = D_n,
\qquad
F_4 = D_4
.
\] Their invariants as \(2\)-elementary lattices are \[
B_n(2) = (n, n, 1),
\quad
C_{4n} = (4n, 2, 0)\ \ (4n\geq 8),
\quad
C_{4n+2} = (4n+2, 2, 1)\ \ (4n+2\geq 6),
\quad
F_4 = (4, 2, 0)
.
\]


Proof. This is (Alexeev 2022, sec. 2).


Remark 36.17 The names on the left refer to the full reflection group of the lattice, generated by reflections in both root lengths, while the names on the right refer to the lattice itself, which is generated by its short roots. The identifications \(D_2 = A_1^{\oplus 2}\) and \(D_3 = A_3\) hold in low rank, and the parabolic diagrams \(\widetilde{A}_n\), \(\widetilde{D}_n\), \(\widetilde{E}_n\) occur in a short version and a long version, the latter written \(\widetilde{A}_n(2)\), \(\widetilde{D}_n(2)\), \(\widetilde{E}_n(2)\); the diagrams \(\widetilde{B}_n\), \(\widetilde{C}_n\) and \(\widetilde{F}_4\) likewise come in two versions, according to which root length dominates (Alexeev 2022, sec. 2). These are the names appearing in the maximal parabolic subdiagrams of Theorem 53.18.

title: 37  Discriminant forms and the genus
text:
Definition 37.2 A quadratic form on a \(\ZZ\)-module \(L\) is a map of sets \(q: L \to \QQ\) such that \(q(\lambda v) = \lambda^2 q(v)\) for all \(v\in L\) and all \(\lambda\in\ZZ\), and whose polar form \(\beta_q\) is a symmetric bilinear form on \(L\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\beta_q: L \tensor_\ZZ L &\to \QQ \\
(v, w) &\mapsto \beta_q(v, w) \definedas q(v+w) - q(v) - q(w)
.
\end{aligned}
\] We say \(q\) is integral if \(q(L) \iscontainedin \ZZ\), and we call the pair \((L, q)\) a quadratic \(\ZZ\)-module.


Remark 37.3 Setting \(w = v\) in the polar form and using homogeneity gives \[
\beta_q(v, v) = q(2v) - 2q(v) = 4q(v) - 2q(v) = 2q(v)
,
\] so that \(q(v) = \tfrac{1}{2}\beta_q(v, v)\). The polar form is thus always even, meaning \(\beta_q(v, v)\in 2\ZZ\) whenever \(q\) is integral. This identity is the source of the bijection recorded below.

title: 37  Discriminant forms and the genus
section: 37.2 The correspondence between bilinear and quadratic forms
text:
37.2 The correspondence between bilinear and quadratic forms

Lemma 37.4 Every \(\QQ\)-valued symmetric bilinear module \((L, \beta)\) determines a \(\QQ\)-valued quadratic module \((L, q_\beta)\) by \[
q_\beta(v) \definedas \beta(v, v)
,
\] and \(q_\beta\) depends only on the symmetric part of \(\beta\). Conversely, every \(\QQ\)-valued quadratic module \((L, q)\) determines a symmetric bilinear module \((L, \beta_q)\) via its polar form from the quadratic-form definition (Definition 37.2).


Lemma 37.5 There is a bijection between even symmetric integral bilinear forms on \(L\) and integral quadratic forms on \(L\): \[
\theset{ \beta\in \Sym^2_\ZZ(\dualof{L}) \mid \beta \text{ is even} }
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
\Quad_\ZZ(L)
,
\] under which a bilinear form \(\beta\) is sent to \(q(v) \definedas \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(v, v)\), and a quadratic form \(q\) is sent to its polar form \(\beta_q\). Note that this forward map \(\beta\mapsto\tfrac{1}{2}\beta(v,v)\) differs by the factor \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) from the map \(\beta\mapsto q_\beta(v) = \beta(v,v)\) of the bilinear/quadratic correspondence lemma (Lemma 37.4), so this bijection is a distinct construction rather than a restriction of that lemma; only the backward (polar-form) direction is shared. Concretely, the polar form of any integral quadratic form is an even symmetric integral bilinear form, and conversely every even symmetric integral bilinear form \(\beta\) is the polar form of the integral quadratic form \(q(v) \definedas \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(v, v)\).


Proof. If \(q\) is integral then \(\beta_q(v, v) = 2q(v)\in 2\ZZ\), so \(\beta_q\) is even and integral. Conversely, if \(\beta\) is even and integral then \(q(v) \definedas \tfrac{1}{2}\beta(v, v)\) takes values in \(\ZZ\), and its polar form recovers \(\beta\): \[
\beta_q(v, w)
= q(v + w) - q(v) - q(w)
= \tfrac{1}{2}\left( \beta(v + w, v + w) - \beta(v, v) - \beta(w, w) \right)
= \beta(v, w)
,
\] using symmetry of \(\beta\). The two assignments are mutually inverse.

title: 37  Discriminant forms and the genus
text:
37.3 Torsion bilinear and quadratic forms

Definition 37.6 A torsion bilinear form is a pair \((G, \beta)\) where \(G\) is a finitely generated torsion \(\ZZ\)-module and \[
\beta: G \tensor_\ZZ G \to \QQ/\ZZ
\] is a symmetric bilinear form. A torsion quadratic form is a pair \((G, q)\) where \(G\) is a finitely generated torsion \(\ZZ\)-module and \(q: G \to \QQ/\ZZ\) is a quadratic form, i.e. \(q(\lambda x) = \lambda^2 q(x)\) for all \(x\in G\) and \(\lambda\in\ZZ\), whose polar form is a torsion bilinear form.


Remark 37.7 The discriminant group \(A_L\) of the Lattice Theory section is a finite, hence finitely generated torsion, \(\ZZ\)-module, so its associated forms are instances of this notion. We record the discriminant data as two separate forms: the discriminant quadratic form \(q_L\colon A_L\to\QQ/2\ZZ\) (matching the \(\QQ/2\ZZ\) normalization of the Lattice Theory section) and the discriminant bilinear form \(b_L\colon A_L\times A_L\to\QQ/\ZZ\). These share the numerator \(\beta(\tilde x,\tilde y)\) read modulo different lattices; the diagonal \(q_L(\bar x) = \beta(\tilde x,\tilde x)\bmod 2\ZZ\) reduces to \(b_L(\bar x,\bar x) = \beta(\tilde x,\tilde x)\bmod\ZZ\) under the natural surjection \(\QQ/2\ZZ\surjects\QQ/\ZZ\), not under any multiplication-by-\(2\) isomorphism.

title: 37  Discriminant forms and the genus
section: 37.4 The discriminant bilinear and quadratic forms
text:
37.4 The discriminant bilinear and quadratic forms

Definition 37.8 Let \((L, \beta_L)\) be a nondegenerate even lattice with discriminant group \(A_L = \dualof{L}/L\), and let \(\beta\) also denote the \(\QQ\)-valued extension of the form to \(\dualof{L}\). The discriminant bilinear form of \(L\) is the torsion bilinear form \[
\begin{aligned}
b_L: A_L \times A_L &\to \QQ/\ZZ \\
(\bar x, \bar y) &\mapsto \beta(x, y) \bmod \ZZ
,
\end{aligned}
\] computed on any lifts \(x, y\in \dualof{L}\) of \(\bar x, \bar y\). Its associated discriminant quadratic form is \[
q_L(\bar x) \definedas \beta(x, x) \bmod 2\ZZ \in \QQ/2\ZZ
,
\] for any lift \(x\) of \(\bar x\); this is the \(\QQ/2\ZZ\)-valued form \(q_L\) recalled from the Lattice Theory section. Reducing modulo \(\ZZ\) recovers the diagonal of \(b_L\), i.e. \(q_L(\bar x)\bmod\ZZ = b_L(\bar x,\bar x)\), via the surjection \(\QQ/2\ZZ\surjects\QQ/\ZZ\). The orthogonal group \(\Orth(A_L)\) is the group of automorphisms of \(A_L\) preserving \(q_L\). The length \(\ell(L)\) of \(L\) is the minimal number of generators of the abelian group \(A_L\).


Remark 37.9 Both \(b_L\) and \(q_L\) are well defined: replacing a lift \(x\) by \(x + m\) with \(m\in L\) changes \(\beta(x, y)\) by \(\beta(m, y)\in\ZZ\) (so \(b_L\) is well defined modulo \(\ZZ\)) and changes \(\beta(x, x)\) by \(\beta(2x, m) + \beta(m, m)\in 2\ZZ\) (so \(q_L\) is well defined modulo \(2\ZZ\)), since \(\beta(\dualof{L}, L)\iscontainedin\ZZ\) and \(L\) is even. These forms are Nikulin’s discriminant forms (Nikulin 1980).


Proposition 37.10 The discriminant forms \(b_L\) and \(q_L\) of a nondegenerate lattice \(L\) are themselves nondegenerate, meaning that \(b_L(\bar x, \,\cdot\,) = 0\) in \(\Hom(A_L, \QQ/\ZZ)\) implies \(\bar x = 0\). For any \(\bar x, \bar y\in A_L\) the \(\QQ/\ZZ\)-valued bilinear form is recovered from the \(\QQ/2\ZZ\)-valued quadratic form by \[
b_L(\bar x, \bar y)
= \tfrac{1}{2}\left( q_L(\bar x + \bar y) - q_L(\bar x) - q_L(\bar y) \right)
,
\] where the bracketed difference lies in \(\QQ/2\ZZ\) and equals \(2\beta(\tilde x, \tilde y)\bmod 2\ZZ\); halving this even representative yields a well-defined element \(\beta(\tilde x, \tilde y)\bmod\ZZ\) of \(\QQ/\ZZ\).


Proof. Nondegeneracy is the statement that the induced map \(A_L \to \Hom(A_L, \QQ/\ZZ)\) is an isomorphism; this holds because \(A_L\) is finite and the pairing \(b_L\) is the pairing induced by the perfect pairing \(\dualof{L}/L \times \dualof{L}/L \to \QQ/\ZZ\) coming from a nondegenerate \(\beta_L\). The polarization identity is the reduction modulo \(\ZZ\) of the identity \(\beta(x, y) = \tfrac{1}{2}(\beta(x + y, x + y) - \beta(x, x) - \beta(y, y))\) on lifts.

title: 37  Discriminant forms and the genus
text:
37.5 Properties of the dual lattice

Proposition 37.11 
Let \(L\) and \(M\) be nondegenerate lattices. The dual lattice \(\dualof{L} = \Hom_\ZZ(L, \ZZ)\) satisfies the following.

Duality commutes with orthogonal direct sums: \(\dualof{(L\oplus M)} = \dualof{L} \oplus \dualof{M}\).
If \(L\) has Gram matrix \(G_\beta\) in a basis \(B_L\), then the dual basis is \(B_{\dualof{L}} = \inverseof{(B_L^t)}\), and the Gram matrix of the dual form is \(G_{\dualof{\beta}} = \inverseof{G_\beta}\).
The discriminant of the dual satisfies \(\operatorname{disc}(\dualof{L}) = 1/\operatorname{disc}(L)\).
The dual of a twist is \(\dualof{(L(m))} = \dualof{L}(1/m)\), where \(L(m)\) is the twist of \(L\) by \(m\) from the Lattice Theory section.



Remark 37.12 Property (2) is the source of (3), since \(\operatorname{disc}(\dualof{L}) = \det(\inverseof{G_\beta}) = 1/\det(G_\beta) = 1/\operatorname{disc}(L)\). Property (1) is compatible with the direct-sum decomposition \(A_{L\oplus M} = A_L\oplus A_M\) of discriminant groups recalled in the Lattice Theory section.
