text:
42.3 The Coble arithmetic group induced from the Enriques side

Definition 42.6 (The induced Coble subgroup) For the Heegner vector \(\delta\) of the explicit Heegner-vector lemma (Lemma 42.2), define \[
\Gamma_\Co^\En(\delta)
\definedas \im\Bigl(
\Stab_{\gent}(\ZZ\delta)
\too
\Orth\bigl(\delta^{\perp \ten}\bigr) = \Orth(T_\Co)
\Bigr)
,
\] the group of restrictions to \(\delta^{\perp}\) of those elements of \(\Gamma_{\En,2}\) that preserve the line \(\ZZ\delta\). The condition is on the line, since a component of the Heegner divisor is determined by \(\ZZ\delta\) and not by a choice of sign for \(\delta\).


Proposition 42.7 (Discriminant description of $\Gamma_{\En, 2}$) Let \(\sen = U(2)\oplus E_8(2)\) and \(\ten\) be the invariant and coinvariant lattices of the Enriques involution on \(\lkt\), and let \[
\gamma\colon A_{\sen}\iso A_{\ten},
\qquad
q_{\ten}\circ\gamma = -q_{\sen}
\] be the gluing anti-isometry supplied by the embedding-gluing description (Remark 38.10) for the primitive embedding \(\sen\injects\lkt\) with complement \(\ten\). Then \[
\gent
= \theset{\,
g_T\in\Orth(\ten)
\;\middle|\;
\exists\, g_S\in\Orth(\sen) \text{ with } g_S(h) = h
\textand \bar g_T\circ\gamma = \gamma\circ\bar g_S
\,}
,
\] where \(h = e + f\in U(2) = \sdp\iscontainedin \sen\) is the degree-\(2\) polarization vector, with \(e^2 = f^2 = 0\) and \(e\cdot f = 2\), so that \(h^2 = 4\) (Alexeev et al. 2025 Def. 2.5, Def. 2.6). Equivalently, the image of \(\Gamma_{\En,2}\) in \(\Orth(q_{T_\En})\) is the \(\gamma\)-transport of the image of \(\Stab_{\Orth(S_\En)}(h)\) in \(\Orth(q_{S_\En})\).


Proof. By definition \(\Gamma_{\En,2}\) is the image in \(\Orth(T_\En)\) of the isometries of \(\lkt\) that commute with \(I_\En\) and fix \(h\) (Alexeev et al. 2025 Def. 2.6). An isometry of \(\lkt\) commuting with \(I_\En\) is the same as a pair \((g_S, g_T)\in\Orth(S_\En)\times\Orth(T_\En)\) preserving the two eigenlattices, and by Nikulin’s gluing theorem (Theorem 38.9) such a pair extends over the overlattice \(\lkt\) of \(S_\En\oplus T_\En\) exactly when it preserves the graph of \(\gamma\), that is when \(\bar g_T\circ\gamma = \gamma\circ\bar g_S\). The polarization \(h\) lies in \(S_\En\), so the condition \(g(h) = h\) on \(\lkt\) is the condition \(g_S(h) = h\).


Proposition 42.8 (The integral stabilizer of the degree-$2$ polarization) Write \(S_\En = C(2)\) with \(C = U\oplus E_8\) even unimodular of signature \((1,9)\), and let \(h\in S_\En\) be the polarization vector of the discriminant description of \(\Gamma_{\En,2}\) (Proposition 42.7), so that \(h = u_0 + w_0\) for a basis \(u_0, w_0\) of the \(U\) summand of \(C\) with \(u_0\cdot w_0 = 1\). Then restriction to \(h^{\perp}\) gives an isomorphism \[
\Stab_{\Orth(S_\En)}(h)
\;\iso\;
\Orth\bigl(\generators{-2}\oplus E_8\bigr)
= \theset{\pm 1}\times W(E_8)
,
\] of order \(2\abs{W(E_8)} = 1\,393\,459\,200\), and the element \(\id_U\oplus(-\id_{E_8})\) lies in the kernel of the reduction \(\Stab_{\Orth(S_\En)}(h)\to\Orth(A_{S_\En}, q_{S_\En})\).


Proof. Twisting does not change the isometry group, so \(\Orth(S_\En) = \Orth(C)\) and \(\Stab_{\Orth(S_\En)}(h) = \Stab_{\Orth(C)}(h)\). Computing in \(C\), one has \(h^2 = 2\) and \(h^{\perp C} = \ZZ(u_0 - w_0)\oplus E_8\) with \((u_0-w_0)^2 = -2\), so \(h^{\perp C}\cong\generators{-2}\oplus E_8\). An isometry fixing \(h\) preserves \(h^{\perp}\), giving the restriction homomorphism, which is injective because \(C_\QQ = \QQ h\oplus h_\QQ^{\perp}\). It is surjective: \(A_{h^{\perp}}\cong A_{\generators{-2}}\cong\ZZ/2\ZZ\) has trivial automorphism group, so every isometry of \(h^{\perp}\) preserves the gluing class of the index-two overlattice \(C\) of \(\ZZ h\oplus h^{\perp}\) and extends over \(C\) fixing \(h\), by Nikulin’s gluing theorem (Theorem 38.9). The lattice \(\generators{-2}\oplus E_8\) is negative definite and generated by its \((-2)\) vectors, whose root system is \(A_1\oplus E_8\); no isometry mixes summands of different ranks, so its isometry group is \(\Orth(\generators{-2})\times\Orth(E_8) = \theset{\pm1}\times W(E_8)\).
For the last claim, \(\id_U\oplus(-\id_{E_8})\) fixes \(h\in U\) and acts on \(A_{S_\En}\cong C/2C\) (the twisted-unimodular discriminant proposition (Proposition 41.6)) by the identity on \(U/2U\) and by \(x\mapsto -x\equiv x\) on \(E_8/2E_8\).


Theorem 42.9 (The finite image and its isotropic orbits) 
With the notation of the polarization-stabilizer proposition (Proposition 42.8) and the explicit Heegner-vector lemma (Lemma 42.2):

the image of the integral stabilizer in the discriminant group, \[
G \definedas \im\bigl(\Stab_{\Orth(S_\En)}(h)\to\Orth(A_{S_\En}, q_{S_\En})\bigr)
,
\] has order \(\abs{W(E_8)} = 696\,729\,600\), and is generated by the swap of the two isotropic generators of the \(U\) summand of \(C\), which fixes \(h\), together with the reflections in the simple roots of the \(E_8\) summand;
the corresponding group \(G_\Co\leq\Orth(A_{T_\Co}, q_{T_\Co})\), obtained by transporting \(G\) along \(\gamma\) and restricting to the Coble Heegner complement \(\delta^{\perp} = T_\Co\), has order \(\abs{W(E_8)}\) and acts on the \(528\) isotropic classes of \(A_{T_\Co}\) with orbit lengths \[
[\,1,\ 2,\ 120,\ 135,\ 270\,]
;
\]
the finite stabilizer \(\Stab_{\Orth(q_{T_\Co})}\bigl(\tfrac12\tilde h_\Co\bigr)\) of the class of the transported polarization has order \(94\,755\,225\,600\), contains \(G_\Co\) with index \(136\), and acts on the same \(528\) isotropic classes with orbit lengths \([\,1,\ 255,\ 272\,]\).



Remark 42.10 (How the three orders are obtained) The generators named in (1) are the two evident families of isometries of \(C\) fixing \(h = u_0 + w_0\): the involution \(u_0\leftrightarrow w_0\), and \(W(E_8)\) acting on the second summand. By the polarization-stabilizer proposition (Proposition 42.8) these generate a group of order \(2\abs{W(E_8)}\) whose reduction has \(\id_U\oplus(-\id_{E_8})\) in its kernel, so the image has order at most \(\abs{W(E_8)}\); the stated equality, and the two orbit decompositions of (2) and (3), are exact computations in the finite quadratic space \(A_{T_\Co}\cong B/2B\) of the Coble mod-four form definition (Definition 41.7), carried out by stabilizing the four fibers of \(Q\) inside \(\GL(B/2B)\) and then computing orbits of the resulting finite group on the fiber \(\inverseof{Q}(0)\). The index \(136 = 94\,755\,225\,600 / 696\,729\,600\) in (3), and the relation \(46\,998\,591\,897\,600 = 496\cdot 94\,755\,225\,600\) between the order of the Coble discriminant-group proposition (Proposition 41.10) and that of the finite stabilizer, are consistency checks: \(\tfrac12\tilde h_\Co\) is a class with \(q_{T_\Co} = 1\), and \(496\) is the number of such classes by the Coble \(Q\)-fiber proposition (Proposition 41.8).


Remark 42.11 (Reading the two orbit decompositions) The two decompositions in the finite-image orbit theorem (Theorem 42.9) answer different questions, and their difference is the content of the theorem. The coarser one, \([1, 255, 272]\), is the decomposition under the whole finite stabilizer of the polarization class, the largest group the discriminant form alone can distinguish. The finer one, \([1, 2, 120, 135, 270]\), is the decomposition under the group that actually arises from integral isometries of \(S_\En\) fixing \(h\), namely \(G_\Co\). Since the latter has index \(136\) in the former, a calculation carried out purely in \(\Orth(q_{T_\Co})\) overestimates how much of \(A_{T_\Co}\) a degree-\(2\) Coble period point can see. The four nonzero orbit lengths \(2, 120, 135, 270\) sum to \(527\), the number of nonzero isotropic classes of the Coble \(Q\)-fiber proposition (Proposition 41.8), so both decompositions refine the single nonzero orbit of the isotropic-class orbit theorem (Theorem 41.11).
Both are statements in the finite quadratic space \(A_{T_\Co}\). Neither is yet a classification of \(\Gamma_\Co^\En(\delta)\)-orbits of primitive isotropic vectors of \(T_\Co\), for the reason recorded in the primitive-isotropic-class proposition (Proposition 41.12): an integral parabolic stabilizer may have proper image in the finite one, so a finite orbit can split.

title: 42  The Heegner line and the Coble arithmetic group
text:
42.4 The Coble folding involution

Proposition 42.12 (The sign involution of the Coble primitive embedding) Let \(S_\Co\injects\lkt\) be the primitive embedding of the Coble invariant-lattice proposition (Proposition 32.4), with complement \(T_\Co = S_\Co^{\perp\lkt}\), and let \[
\gamma_\Co\colon A_{S_\Co}\iso A_{T_\Co},
\qquad
q_{T_\Co}\circ\gamma_\Co = -q_{S_\Co}
\] be the associated gluing anti-isometry. Then the pair \((-\id_{S_\Co}, \id_{T_\Co})\) preserves the graph of \(\gamma_\Co\) and therefore defines an isometry \[
\theta_\Co\in\Orth(\lkt),
\qquad
\restrictionof{\theta_\Co}{S_\Co} = -\id,
\qquad
\restrictionof{\theta_\Co}{T_\Co} = \id
,
\] whose \((+1)\) and \((-1)\) eigenlattices are \(T_\Co\) and \(S_\Co\). An isometry of \(\lkt\) commutes with \(\theta_\Co\) if and only if it preserves both eigenlattices.


Proof. Both \(A_{S_\Co}\) and \(A_{T_\Co}\) are \(2\)-elementary, so \(-\id\) and \(\id\) agree on each of them; the pair therefore acts as the identity on the graph of \(\gamma_\Co\) and by Nikulin’s gluing theorem (Theorem 38.9) extends over the overlattice \(\lkt\) of \(S_\Co\oplus T_\Co\). The eigenlattice description is the definition of the extension. For the last claim, an isometry commuting with an involution preserves its eigenspaces, which by the involution-eigenspace proposition (Proposition 40.3) are the rational spans of \(T_\Co\) and \(S_\Co\); conversely an isometry preserving both eigenlattices commutes with \(\theta_\Co\) on each of them and hence on \(\lkt\).


Remark 42.13 The folding-involution proposition (Proposition 42.12) settles the existence of the folding involution \(\theta\) as a lattice isometry, and does so before any \(22\times 22\) matrix is written: the involution is determined by the primitive embedding and the gluing anti-isometry. What a matrix realization additionally supplies is a basis in which \(\theta_\Co\), the polarization class, and the roots of the Coxeter diagram can be compared with one another.
Combining the folding-involution proposition (Proposition 42.12) with the discriminant description of \(\Gamma_{\En,2}\) (Proposition 42.7) gives the Coble-side analogue of the discriminant description of \(\Gamma_{\En,2}\): the restriction to \(T_\Co\) of the centralizer of \(\theta_\Co\) inside the stabilizer of a chosen polarization class \(\tilde h_\Co\in S_\Co\) consists of those \(g_T\in\Orth(T_\Co)\) for which some \(g_S\in\Orth(S_\Co)\) satisfies \(g_S(\tilde h_\Co) = \tilde h_\Co\) and \(\bar g_T\circ\gamma_\Co = \gamma_\Co\circ\bar g_S\). Identifying that group with \(\Gamma_\Co^\En(\delta)\) of the induced Coble subgroup definition (Definition 42.6) requires an isometry between the Coble primitive embedding and the Enriques Heegner complement carrying \(\tilde h_\Co\) to the class \(h = e+f\) of the discriminant description of \(\Gamma_{\En,2}\) (Proposition 42.7). The images of the two groups in \(\Orth(q_{T_\Co})\) do agree, by the finite-image orbit theorem (Theorem 42.9), but agreement of finite images is weaker than an isomorphism of the lattice subgroups.





Alexeev, Valery, Philip Engel, D. Zack Garza, and Luca Schaffler. 2025. “Compact Moduli of Enriques Surfaces with a Numerical Polarization of Degree 2.” Nagoya Mathematical Journal.


Dawes, Matthew. 2022. Orbits in Lattices. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2205.10601.


Dolgachev, Igor, and Shigeyuki Kondō. 2013. “The Rationality of the Moduli Spaces of Coble Surfaces and of Nodal Enriques Surfaces.” Izvestiya: Mathematics 77.

Notation 43.2 (Notation for the discriminant representation) For a lattice \(L\) the induced homomorphism \[
\rho_L\colon \Orth(L)\too \Orth(q_L)
\] of the Lattice Theory section, sending an isometry to its action on the discriminant form, is the discriminant representation of \(L\). Its kernel is the stable orthogonal group \(\tilde\Orth(L)\), and we write \(\bar\varphi\definedas\rho_L(\varphi)\). The homomorphism exists because an isometry of \(L\) extends to a \(\ZZ\)-module isomorphism of \(\dualof{L}\) and so descends to \(A_L = \dualof{L}/L\) (Nikulin 1980, sec. 1.4).


Remark 43.3 For an orthogonal direct sum, \(A_{M\oplus N} = A_M\oplus A_N\) and \(\rho_{M\oplus N}(\varphi_M\oplus\varphi_N) = \bar\varphi_M\oplus\bar\varphi_N\), by the additivity of discriminant groups recorded in the Lattice Theory section.

title: 43  Automorphism lifting through a gluing
text:
43.2 The lifting criterion

Definition 43.4 (The gluing datum of a pair of primitive inclusions) Let \(\iota_M\colon M\injects L\) and \(\iota_N\colon N\injects L\) be primitive inclusions with \(\iota_N(N) = \iota_M(M)^{\perp L}\), so that \(L\) is an even overlattice of \(M\oplus N\). The gluing datum of the pair is the isotropic subgroup \[
H \definedas L/(M\oplus N) \ \leq\ A_M\oplus A_N
\] attached to \(L\) by Theorem 38.9, together with the two inclusions themselves. By Remark 38.10 the subgroup \(H\) is the graph of an anti-isometry \(\gamma\colon H_M\iso H_N\) between subgroups \(H_M\leq A_M\) and \(H_N\leq A_N\), and \(L\) is recovered as the preimage of \(H\) under the quotient map \(\dualof{(M\oplus N)}\to A_M\oplus A_N\).


Theorem 43.5 (When a pair of isometries lifts) Let \(L\), \(M\), \(N\) and \(H\) be as in the gluing-datum definition (Definition 43.4), and let \(\varphi_M\in\Orth(M)\) and \(\varphi_N\in\Orth(N)\). Then \(\varphi_M\oplus\varphi_N\) extends to an isometry of \(L\) if and only if \[
\left(\bar\varphi_M\oplus\bar\varphi_N\right)(H) = H
.
\] The extension is then unique, and it restricts to \(\varphi_M\) on \(M\) and to \(\varphi_N\) on \(N\).


Proof. Write \(\psi\definedas\varphi_M\oplus\varphi_N\in\Orth(M\oplus N)\). An isometry of \(M\oplus N\) extends uniquely to a \(\ZZ\)-module isometry \(\dualof{\psi}\) of \(\dualof{(M\oplus N)}\) inside \((M\oplus N)\tensor_\ZZ\QQ\), so the only candidate extension to \(L\) is \(\restrictionof{\dualof{\psi}}{L}\), and uniqueness follows. Since \(M\oplus N\iscontainedin L\dualof{\iscontainedin(M\oplus N)}\) by Definition 38.8, the candidate maps \(L\) into \(\dualof{(M\oplus N)}\) always, and preserves \(L\) exactly when it preserves the image of \(L\) in the quotient \(A_{M\oplus N} = A_M\oplus A_N\). That image is \(H\), and the induced action of \(\dualof{\psi}\) on \(A_{M\oplus N}\) is \(\bar\varphi_M\oplus\bar\varphi_N\), giving the stated condition. Conversely, if the condition holds then \(\restrictionof{\dualof{\psi}}{L}\) is a bijection of \(L\) preserving the form inherited from \((M\oplus N)\tensor_\ZZ\QQ\), hence an isometry of \(L\).


Corollary 43.6 (The liftable subgroup) With the notation of the lifting criterion (Theorem 43.5), fix \(\varphi_N = \id_N\) and let \(\Gamma\leq\Orth(M)\) be any subgroup. The isometries of \(M\) that extend over \(L\) fixing \(N\) pointwise form the subgroup \[
\inverseof{\rho_M}\Bigl(\Stab_{\Orth(q_M)}(H)\Bigr)\ \intersect\ \Gamma
\ \leq\ \Gamma
,
\] where \(\Stab_{\Orth(q_M)}(H)\) is the stabilizer of \(H\) for the action of \(\Orth(q_M)\) on subgroups of \(A_M\oplus A_N\) through the first summand. In particular the liftable subgroup contains \(\tilde\Orth(M)\intersect\Gamma\), and it has finite index in \(\Gamma\) whenever \(\rho_M(\Gamma)\) is finite.


Proof. Apply the lifting criterion (Theorem 43.5) with \(\bar\varphi_N = \id\), so that the condition reads \((\bar\varphi_M\oplus\id)(H) = H\); the set of \(\bar\varphi_M\) satisfying it is by definition the stabilizer, which is a subgroup of \(\Orth(q_M)\), and its preimage under the homomorphism \(\rho_M\) is a subgroup of \(\Orth(M)\). The stable orthogonal group is the kernel of \(\rho_M\) (the discriminant-representation notation (Notation 43.2)) and so acts trivially on \(H\). Finiteness of the index follows because \(\Orth(q_M)\) is finite, \(A_M\) being finite.


Remark 43.7 (The operation belongs to the arrow) The datum consumed by the lifting criterion (Theorem 43.5) is \(H\), equivalently the pair of primitive inclusions of the gluing-datum definition (Definition 43.4). Neither \(M\) nor \(N\) determines it: the same lattice \(M\) occurs in many gluings, and each one imposes its own condition. Liftability is therefore a property of the inclusions, and the subgroup of the liftable-subgroup corollary (Corollary 43.6) is attached to them.
The hypotheses are morphism-level for the same reason. An inclusion is primitive when its cokernel is torsion-free (Proposition 38.3), and saturation and index are properties of the inclusion; a determinant or a greatest common divisor of matrix entries recognizes primitivity only under hypotheses that the definition itself does not state.

43.3 The unimodular case and its two specimens

Corollary 43.8 (Lifting across a unimodular overlattice) Suppose in addition that \(L\) is unimodular. Then \(H\) is the graph of an anti-isometry \(\gamma\colon A_M\iso A_N\) defined on all of \(A_M\), and \(\varphi_M\oplus\varphi_N\) extends to \(L\) if and only if \[
\bar\varphi_N\circ\gamma = \gamma\circ\bar\varphi_M
.
\]


Proof. Unimodularity of \(L\) forces \(H_M = A_M\) and \(H_N = A_N\) in Remark 38.10, so \(H\) is the graph \(\theset{(x, \gamma x) \mid x\in A_M}\) of an anti-isometry defined on all of \(A_M\). A pair preserves that graph exactly when \(\bar\varphi_N(\gamma x) = \gamma(\bar\varphi_M x)\) for every \(x\), which is the displayed identity.


Remark 43.9 (Two computations in this book are instances) The unimodular lifting corollary (Corollary 43.8) is the mechanism behind two statements proved elsewhere in this part, both for the unimodular \(\lkt\).
The discriminant description of the degree-\(2\) Enriques group (Proposition 42.7) is the liftable-subgroup computation of the liftable-subgroup corollary (Corollary 43.6) for the gluing \(\sen\oplus \ten\iscontainedin\lkt\), with the extra condition \(g_S(h) = h\) cutting \(\Gamma\leq\Orth(\sen)\) down to the stabilizer of the polarization; the commutation identity \(\bar g_T\circ\gamma = \gamma\circ\bar g_S\) appearing there is exactly the criterion above.
The Coble folding involution (Proposition 42.12) is the same criterion applied to the pair \((-\id_{S_\Co}, \id_{T_\Co})\) for the gluing \(S_\Co\oplus T_\Co\iscontainedin\lkt\): because both discriminant groups are \(2\)-elementary, \(\overline{-\id} = \overline{\id}\) on each, and the identity holds trivially, so the pair lifts.





Nikulin, V. V. 1980. “Integral Symmetric Bilinear Forms and Some of Their Applications.” Mathematics of the USSR-Izvestiya 14 (1): 103. https://doi.org/10.1070/IM1980v014n01ABEH001060.

title: 44  Coble lattices
text:
The following can be found in an unpublished note of Dolgachev.1 Write \(\abs{-2K_S} = \theset{C}\) where \(C = C_1 + \cdots + C_n\) has \(n\) irreducible components. By adjunction, \(C_i\cong \PP^1\) and \(C_i^2 = -4\), so \(K_S^2 = -n\). Let \(\Sigma\) be a general Coble set of points in \(\PP^2\). There are 10 irreducible families of K3s obtained as the double cover of \(S\) branched over \(C\), where the fixed point locus of the deck transformation consists of \(n\) smooth rational curves. Generally the rank of \(\Pic(X)\) is \(r=10+n\) and \(\ell = 12-n\), and \(K_S^2 = 9 - \abs{\Sigma} = -n\).
This table is reproduced in (Cossec et al. 2025 Table 5.1, p.553). The fixed point locus is described by (Cossec et al. 2025 Eqn. 5.3.1):
\[
X^{g}=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\emptyset & \text { if }(r, l, \delta)=\EnriquesInvariants, \\
C_{1}^{(1)}+C_{2}^{(1)} & \text { if }(r, l, \delta)=(10,8,0), \\
C^{(g)}+\Sum_{i=1}^{k} R_{i} & \text { otherwise }
\end{array}\right.
\]
where \(C^{(g)}\) denotes a curve of genus \(g \geq 0\), \(R_{i}\) are disjoint \((-2)\)-curves, and \[g=\frac{1}{2}(22-r-l), \quad k=\frac{1}{2}(r-l).\]
The ramification divisor for the involution on the K3 cover is described by \(g=0\) and \(k=n-1\) by (Cossec et al. 2025 Def. 5.4.3).

title: 47  Constructions of the moduli space
text:
47.1 The GIT construction
We summarize the relevant moduli spaces:
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_\En &= \bD(T_\En)/\Orth^+(T_\En)^* &
\fentwo &= \bD(T_\En)/\Gamma_{\En, 2} \\
F_\Co &= \bD(T_\Co) / \Orth^+(T_\Co)^* &
F_{\Co, 2} &= \bD(T_\Co)/\Gamma_{\Co, 2}
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma_{\En, 2} &= \Orth(T_\En) \intersect \Orth(\tdp) \iscontainedin \Orth(\lkt) \\
\Gamma_{\Co, 2} &= \mathrm{Stab}_{\Orth(T_\En)}(T_\Co) \iscontainedin \Orth(T_\En) \\
F_{\Nod} &= \bD(T_\Nod)/\Orth^+(T_\Nod)^* \\
F_{\Nod, 2} &= ???
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\tdp\) is described in (Alexeev et al. 2025). Note that we implicitly use the embedding \(\eta: T_\Co \injects T_\En\) of the primitive-embedding lemma (Lemma 48.1).
We note, as in (Dolgachev and Kondō 2013), that \(T_{\Co} \cong v^{\perp \ten}\) for some \(v^2=-2\), which implies that there is a birational isomorphism \(\fco \birationaliso \mch_{-2}/\Orth^+(\ten)^*\).
The tower relates the degree-\(2\) numerically polarized Coble and Enriques moduli \(F_{\Co,2}\), \(\fentwo\), their unpolarized quotients \(\fco\), \(F_\En\), and the degree-\((2,2,0)\) K3 moduli space \(F_{(2,2,0)}\injects F_4\). The map \(F_{\Co,2}\to F_\Co\) marked \(?\) is the one not yet determined, for the reason above: \(\Gamma_{\Co,2}\) has no explicit description.

title: 47  Constructions of the moduli space
text:
Remark 47.2 (GIT construction) Following (Dolgachev and Kondō 2013), by varying the coefficients of \(p_i\) in the planar blowup construction, one can construct \(F_\Co\) as a locally closed subvariety of \((\PP^2)^{10}/\PGL_3\), which is of dimension
\[
\dim (\PP^2)^{10}/\PGL_3 = \dim (\PP^2)^{10} - \dim \PGL_3 = 2\cdot 10 - (3^2-1) = 12
.
\]
A posteriori, the number of moduli for a Coble surface is 9, which means that there should be 3 conditions imposed upon the configuration of 10 points. These 3 conditions are precisely the discriminant conditions described in (Coble 1919, sec. 2, Prop. (10)). Letting \(D\) be the corresponding discriminant locus, we can identify \(\fco\) as an open subset of \(\qty{ (\PP^2)^{10} \sm D }/\PGL_3\) at the level of coarse moduli spaces.
crumbs: 47  Constructions of the moduli space

title: 47  Constructions of the moduli space
text:
47.2 The Horikawa model

Remark 47.3 (Horikawa's construction) Alternatively, Horikawa (Horikawa 1977) and more recently (Alexeev et al. 2025) consider the following: let \(Y\definedas \PP^1\times \PP^1\) and define an involution \(\tau(x,y) \definedas (-x,-y)\). Letting \(B\in\abs{-2K_Y}^\tau\) be a \(\tau\)-invariant anti-bicanonical curve in \(Y\), if \(B\) passes through a \(\tau\)-fixed point \(x,y\in \theset{0, \pm \infty}\), then the corresponding double branched cover branched over \(B\) is a nodal K3 surface \(X\) with \(A_1\) singularities and covering involution \(\idp\) such that \(Y = X/\generators{\idp}\). Letting \(\ien\) be a lift of \(\tau\), the quotient \(Z\definedas X/\generators{\ien}\) is a Coble surface. The case in which \(B\) does not pass through a \(\tau\)-invariant point yields an Enriques surface \(Z\), and an analysis of the corresponding moduli is carried out in (Alexeev et al. 2025).
It is well-known that there consequently exists a Coble surface \(S\) and a blowdown \(S\to X/\iota\) along the strict transform of \(B\). In this way, one realizes the moduli space \(\fco\) of unpolarized Coble surfaces as a divisor in \(\fen\), the 10-dimensional moduli space of unpolarized Enriques surfaces.
crumbs: 47  Constructions of the moduli space

title: 47  Constructions of the moduli space
text:
47.3 Period domains
By passing to the K3 cover, one can embed \(F_\Co\) into an arithmetic quotient of a 9-dimensional Hermitian symmetric domain of type \(\rm{IV}\). Let \(\lkt = U^3 \oplus E_8^2\) be the canonical K3 lattice. We recall that for any primitively embedded lattice \(S\injects \lkt\), letting \(T \definedas S^{\perp \lkt}\), there is a Hodge-theoretic description of the coarse moduli space \(F_S\) of \(S\)-polarized K3 surfaces given by \[F_S \definedas D_T/\Orth^+(T)^*\]
where \(\Orth^+(T)^* \definedas \Orth^+(T) \intersect \ker\qty{\Orth(T) \to \Orth(q_T)}\), the group \(\Orth^+(T)\) is the index-two subgroup of \(\Orth(T)\) preserving the component \(D_T\), and \(D_T\) is a connected component of
\[
\Omega_T \definedas \theset{[v]\in \PP(T_\CC) \st v^2=0,\, v\bar v > 0}
.
\]

Proposition 47.4 (Dimension of a type IV domain) Let \(T\) be a lattice of rank \(r\) and signature \((2, r-2)\). Then the type IV domain \(D_T\) has complex dimension \(r - 2\).


Proof. The complexification \(T_\CC\) has dimension \(r\), so \(\PP(T_\CC)\) has dimension \(r-1\). The equation \(v^2 = 0\) is a single nondegenerate quadratic equation and cuts out a smooth quadric hypersurface of dimension \(r-2\) inside \(\PP(T_\CC)\). The condition \(v\bar v > 0\) is open, so it selects an open subset of that quadric, and \(D_T\) is one of its connected components.


Corollary 47.5 (Dimension of $M$-polarized K3 moduli) Let \(M\injects\lkt\) be a primitive embedding of a lattice of signature \((1, \rank(M) - 1)\) with orthogonal complement \(T = M^{\perp\lkt}\). Then \[
\dim_\CC D_T = \rank(T) - 2 = 20 - \rank(M)
.
\] For the Coble lattices \(\rank(S_\Co) = 11\), so \(\dim_\CC D_{T_\Co} = 9\).


Proof. The K3 lattice has rank \(22\), so \(\rank(T) = 22 - \rank(M)\), and \(T\) has signature \((2, 20 - \rank(M))\); apply the type-IV dimension proposition (Proposition 47.4).

Letting \(E_{10} \definedas U \oplus E_8\), one can similarly consider the Enriques lattices \(S_\En := E_{10}(2)\) with \(T_\En = U \oplus E_{10}(2)\). Letting
\[
\mch_{-2d} = \Union_{\delta^2 = -2d} \delta^{\perp D_T}
,
\]
be the union of the hyperplane sections cut out by the vectors \(\delta\) of norm \(-2d\), as in Figure 47.1, one can thus present
\[
\begin{aligned}
\fen &= \qty{D_{T_\En} \sm \mch_{-2}} / \Orth^+(T_\En)^* \\
\fco &= \mch_{-2} / \Orth^+(T_\En)^* \\
F_{\Nod} &= \qty{\mch_{-4} \sm \mch_{-2}} / \Orth^+(T_\En)^*
\end{aligned}
\]
where surfaces along the divisor \(\mch_{-2}\) in \(\fen\) correspond precisely to Coble surfaces and those along \(\mch_{-4}\sm \mch_{-2}\) correspond to Enriques surfaces with \(A_1\) singularities.




































































































Figure 47.1: The period domain \(D_{T_\En}\) together with the hyperplanes \(v_i^{\perp}\) cut out by vectors \(v_i\) of fixed negative norm. The Coble surfaces are precisely the periods lying on the hyperplanes of \(\mch_{-2}\).



Alternatively, one can construct the period domain for \(F_\Co\) directly. Following (Dolgachev and Kondō 2013 Prop. 3.1) almost verbatim, let \(S\) be the blowup of \(\PP^2\) along 10 \(A_1\) singularities of a rational sextic curve \(C\). The double branched cover \(f:X\to S\) branched along the proper transform of \(C\) contains the pullback of ten exceptional classes \(E_1,\cdots, E_{10}\) over the ten \(A_1\) singularities, as well as \(E_0\), the pullback of a hyperplane class. Since \(E_i^2 = -2\) for \(1\leq i \leq 10\), and one can show that \(E_0^2 = 2\), the \(E_i\) generate a lattice isometric to
\[
S_\Co \definedas \generators{2}\oplus \generators{-2}^{10} = \latI_{1, 10}(2) = (11, 11, 1)_1 \cong \generators{-2} \oplus E_{10}(2)
.
\]
This follows from the fact that \(S_{\Co}\) is a 2-elementary lattice of signature \((1, 10)\) with discriminant group \((\bZ/2\bZ)^{11}\) and thus uniquely determined up to isometry by its invariants \((r,a,\delta)\). Similarly, its orthogonal complement \(T_{\Co}\) in the K3 lattice \(\lkt\) is a 2-elementary lattice of signature \((2, 9)\) and satisfies \(q_{S_{\Co}} = -q_{T_{\Co}}\). The isomorphism class of \(q_{T_{\Co}}\) determines \(T_\Co\), and thus one has
\[
T_\Co \definedas S_\Co^{\perp \lkt} = (11, 11, 1)_2 \cong \generators{2} \oplus E_{10}(2)
.
\]
Alternatively, this follows immediately from the mirror move \(S\leadsto T\) of (Alexeev and Engel 2022 Thm. 5.10) applied to \(S_\Co =(11, 11, 1)_1\). We obtain \(F_\Co\) as an open subset of the period domain \(D_{T_\Co}/\Orth^+(T_\Co)^*\), a normal quasiprojective variety of dimension 9, by (Dolgachev and Kondō 2013 Prop. 3.2) and an application of the Torelli theorem for algebraic K3 surfaces from (Piatetski-Shapiro and Shafarevich 1971). We note that (Dolgachev and Kondō 2013) shows that \(F_\Co\) is rational by relating it to a codimension one subvariety of a moduli space of certain \(A_2\)-singular quintics in \(\PP^2\).
crumbs: 47  Constructions of the moduli space

title: 47  Constructions of the moduli space
text:
47.4 The sextic moduli construction

Remark 47.6 (Orientation) The constructions above start from the surface: from the Coble surface \(S\) and its K3 cover, or from the Enriques period domain in which the Coble locus is a Heegner divisor. A third route starts from the branch curve and never mentions \(S\): one takes the moduli space of plane sextics of a fixed singularity type, and maps it to an arithmetic quotient by the periods of the associated K3. Yu–Zheng–Zhong carry this out for every singular type \(T\) of plane sextic with simple singularities (Yu et al. 2025), and the Coble case is the type \(T = 10A_1\). What this route supplies that the two above do not is a compactification of the open moduli space by geometry of the curves, namely the geometric invariant theory quotient, together with an identification of that compactification in arithmetic terms.


Notation 47.7 (Moduli of sextics of a fixed singular type) For a singular type \(T\) with root lattice \(R\), write \(\mcv_T\) for the space of sextic curves \(Z\subset\PP^2\) with singularities exactly of type \(T\), and \[
\mcm_T \definedas \PP\mcv_T \modmod \SL_3
\] for the moduli space of such curves, the quotient being taken in the sense of geometric invariant theory (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 2.1). Let \(\wh X\) be the double cover of \(\PP^2\) branched along \(Z\), let \(X\) be its minimal resolution — a K3 surface — and let \(H\in\Pic(X)\) be the pullback of the line class, so \(H^2 = 2\). The exceptional curves of \(X\to\wh X\) span a copy \(L\iscontainedin\Pic(X)\) of the root lattice \(R\), with the exceptional classes as a base \(\Delta\). Write \(P\) for the primitive hull of \(\generators H\oplus L\) in \(H^2(X;\ZZ)\) and \(Q \definedas P^{\perp}\), of signatures \((1,\rank R)\) and \((2, 19 - \rank R)\) (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 2.3). For a general member of \(\mcv_T\) one has \(\Pic(X) = P\) (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 3.3).


Proposition 47.8 (The Coble lattices are the lattices of the type $10A_1$) Let \(Z\) be an irreducible sextic of type \(T = 10A_1\), so that \(Z\) is rational by the ten-nodal-sextic lemma (Lemma 34.1), and \(X\) is the K3 cover of the Coble surface \(S = X/\iota\). Then \[
P = \generators{H}\oplus A_1^{\oplus 10} \cong \latI_{1,10}(2) = S_\Co,
\qquad
Q = P^{\perp\lkt} = T_\Co
.
\] In particular \(\dim D(Q) = 9\).


Proof. The saturation of \(\generators H\oplus L\) inside \(H^2(X;\ZZ)\) is \((\ZZ/2)^{l'-1}\), where \(l'\) is the number of irreducible components of \(Z\) (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 5.3); for an irreducible sextic \(l' = 1\), so no saturation occurs and \(P = \generators H\oplus L\). With \(H^2 = 2\) and \(L = A_1^{\oplus 10} = \generators{-2}^{\oplus 10}\) this is \(\generators 2\oplus\generators{-2}^{\oplus 10} = \latI_{1,10}(2)\), which is \(S_\Co\) by the Coble invariant-lattice proposition (Proposition 32.4). Taking orthogonal complements in \(\lkt\) gives \(Q = T_\Co\), and the polarized-K3 dimension corollary (Corollary 47.5) gives the dimension.


Remark 47.9 (The involution acts trivially on the root lattice) For a general singular type the covering involution \(\iota\) acts on \(L\) by \(-w_0(L)\), where \(w_0\) is the longest element of \(W(L)\) (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 5.2), and this action folds the root lattice. For \(L\) of type \(A_1\) one has \(-w_0 = \id\), so in the type \(10A_1\) the involution fixes \(L\) pointwise and no folding occurs; the sublattice of \(H^2(S;\ZZ)\) spanned by the exceptional classes of \(S\to\PP^2\) then becomes \(L\) after scaling by \(2\) (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 5.3). That is the same twist by \(2\) recorded geometrically in the K3-cover twist remark (Remark 32.5): the Coble Picard lattice is the blowup lattice \(\latI_{1,10}\) scaled by \(2\), with no folding correction.


Theorem 47.10 (The occult period map and its image) Let \(\Gamma_T\) be the image of \[
\Orth\bigl(H^2(X;\ZZ),\, \Delta,\, H\bigr) \too \Orth(Q)
,
\] restricted to the subgroup preserving a chosen component \(D(Q)\); it is arithmetic of finite index in \(\Orth(Q)\), and contains every isometry of \(Q\) acting trivially on \(A_Q\) (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 3.1). The occult period map \[
\mathscr P_T\colon \mcm_T \too \Gamma_T\backslash D(Q)
\] is an algebraic open embedding with image \(\Gamma_T\backslash\bigl(D(Q) - \mch_T\bigr)\), where \(\mch_T\) is the arrangement of hyperplanes \(r^{\perp}\) for roots \(r\) orthogonal to \(H\) and not lying in \(L\). When \(T\) is a nodal type, \(\mathscr P_T\) is moreover an isomorphism of orbifolds onto \(P\Gamma_T\backslash(D(Q) - \mch_T)\) (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 1, §3.2, §3.3, §6.2). The description of the image restates, at the level of moduli spaces, the equisingular deformation theory of Urabe (Urabe 1988).


Theorem 47.11 (The GIT compactification is a Looijenga compactification) Let \(\Lambda_1 \definedas H^{\perp\lkt}\), of signature \((2,19)\) with \(A_{\Lambda_1}\cong\ZZ/2\), and let \(\Gamma_1\) be the arithmetic group of the degree-\(2\) K3 moduli space \(\Gamma_1\backslash D(\Lambda_1)\). The roots of \(\Lambda_1\) fall into two \(\Gamma_1\)-orbits, of divisibility \(1\) and \(2\), cutting out arrangements \(\mch_\Delta\) and \(\mch_\infty\); the roots of \(L\) all have divisibility \(1\), so they contribute to \(\mch_\Delta\) only (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 4.1, §4.2). Set \[
\mch^{*}_T \definedas \mch_\infty \intersect D(Q) \iscontainedin \mch_T
.
\] Then \(\mathscr P_T\) extends to an isomorphism \[
\wh{\mcm}_T \;\cong\; \overline{\Gamma_T\backslash D(Q)}^{\,\mch^{*}_T}
\] between the GIT compactification of \(\mcm_T\) and the Looijenga compactification (the Looijenga-compactification definition (Definition 54.11)) of \(\Gamma_T\backslash(D(Q) - \mch^{*}_T)\), compatibly with the corresponding statement of Shah and Looijenga for the whole space of sextics, \(\overline{\mcm}\cong\overline{\Gamma_1\backslash D(\Lambda_1)}^{\,\mch_\infty}\) (Shah 1980; Looijenga 2002); the two vertical maps of the resulting square are normalizations onto their images (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 4.2).


Remark 47.12 (The arithmetic group as a normalizer) \(\Gamma_T\) admits a second description: it is the restriction to \(Q\) of the normalizer of the Weyl group \(W(L)\) inside \(\Gamma_1\) (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 4.2). For \(T = 10A_1\) this reads \[
W(L) = \theset{\pm 1}^{10},
\qquad
\Gamma_{10A_1} = \Gamma_W|_{Q},
\qquad
\Gamma_W = N_{\Gamma_1}\bigl(\theset{\pm1}^{10}\bigr)
,
\] and the normalizer contains the permutations of the ten nodes, so the induced action on \(A_P\cong(\ZZ/2)^{11}\) is through \(\mathfrak S_{10}\). This is a description of an arithmetic group acting on \(D(T_\Co)\) obtained from the ambient degree-\(2\) K3 group rather than from the Enriques side, and it is therefore independent of the description of \(\Gamma_\Co\) as a stabilizer and centralizer inside \(\Orth(T_\En)\) recorded in the Open Problems section.


Question 47.13 (Which quotient of $D(T_\Co)$ is $F_\Co$?) \(F_\Co\) is defined above as an open subset of \(D(T_\Co)/\Orth^+(T_\Co)^*\), a quotient by the stable orthogonal group, whereas \(\mcm_{10A_1}\) is a quotient by \(\Gamma_{10A_1}\), which contains \(\Orth^+(T_\Co)^*\) and may be strictly larger. Identifying the two constructions of the Coble moduli space therefore requires the comparison \[
\Orth^+(T_\Co)^* \;\iscontainedin\; \Gamma_{10A_1} \;\iscontainedin\; \Orth(T_\Co)
,
\] together with the comparison of both against the polarized group \(\Gamma_{\Co,2}\). Until the first inclusion is shown to be an equality, \(\mcm_{10A_1}\) and \(F_\Co\) are two arithmetic quotients of the same period domain by two different groups, not the same space under two names.


Remark 47.14 (The other singular types) The same theorems hold for every singular type of plane sextic with simple singularities, of which the root lattices have been classified by Urabe (Urabe 1988) and Yang (Yang 1996): the maximal rank is \(19\), and the number of root lattices of rank \(19\), \(18\), \(17\), \(16\) is \(519\), \(987\), \(975\), \(782\) respectively (Yu et al. 2025, sec. 1). Each such type therefore carries both an arithmetic model of its moduli space and a Looijenga model of its GIT compactification. The Coble families with \(n\) boundary components are indexed by the number of irreducible components of the branch sextic (the Coble lattice table) rather than by its singular type, so which type \(T\) carries which family is a question this section does not settle.

text:
47.5 KSBA spaces

Remark 47.15 By the Baily–Borel extension lemma (Lemma 48.3), there are morphisms \(\overline{\fco}^{\bb} \to \overline{\fen}^{\bb}\) and \(\overline{\fco}^{\bb} \to \overline{F_{(2,2,0)}}^{\bb}\) which induce correspondences between the boundary cusps.


Remark 47.16 We set up the moduli space of KSBA stable pairs for Coble surfaces, possibly using the ramification divisor of the K3 involution (which is in this case not fixed-point free). The above embeddings should allow us to take closures of stable pairs in already existing moduli spaces.

text: 49.1 Reflections and the Weyl group
crumbs: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg's algorithm

title: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg’s algorithm
text:
Definition 49.2 Let \((L,\beta_L)\) be a nondegenerate integral lattice and \(\alpha\in L\) an anisotropic vector (that is, \(\beta_L(\alpha,\alpha)\neq 0\)) satisfying the integrality condition \[
2\,\beta_L(\alpha, L) \iscontainedin \beta_L(\alpha,\alpha)\,\ZZ
.
\] The reflection in \(\alpha\) is the isometry \[
\begin{aligned}
s_\alpha : L &\to L \\
x &\mapsto x - 2\,\frac{\beta_L(\alpha,x)}{\beta_L(\alpha,\alpha)}\,\alpha
.
\end{aligned}
\] Each reflection has determinant \(-1\), fixes the orthogonal complement \(\generators{\alpha}^{\perp L}\) pointwise, and sends \(\alpha\mapsto -\alpha\). The integrality condition is exactly what guarantees \(s_\alpha\in\Orth(L)\) rather than merely \(s_\alpha\in\Orth(L_\QQ)\). The Weyl group of \(L\) is the subgroup \[
W(L) \definedas \generators{\, s_\alpha \mid \alpha\in L \text{ anisotropic},\ s_\alpha\in\Orth(L) \,}
\leq \Orth(L)
\] generated by all such integral reflections.
crumbs: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg's algorithm

title: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg’s algorithm
text:
49.2 Roots and \(k\)-roots

Definition 49.3 Let \(L\) be a nondegenerate integral lattice and \(v\in L\) a primitive vector. The reflection \(s_v\) is always an isometry of \(L_\QQ\), but is integral, \(s_v\in\Orth(L)\), precisely when \[
2\,\beta_L(v, L) \iscontainedin v^2\,\ZZ
.
\] For \(k>0\) the \(k\)-Weyl group \(W^k(L)\) is the subgroup generated by the integral reflections \(s_v\) with \(v^2 = -k\): \[
W^k(L) \definedas \generators{\, s_v \mid s_v\in\Orth(L),\ v^2 = -k \,}
.
\] A vector \(v\) is a \(k\)-root if \(s_v\in W^k(L)\). The full Weyl group \(W(L)\) of Definition 49.2 is generated by integral reflections in vectors of any norm, so that \(W(L) = \generators{\, W^k(L) \mid k>0 \,}\).


Definition 49.4 
For a \(2\)-elementary lattice \(L\), the roots are precisely the vectors \(v\in L\) of one of the two following types:

a short root, with \(v^2 = -2\); or
a long root, with \(v^2 = -4\) and \(\div_L(v) = 2\).



Remark 49.5 The two root types of Definition 49.4 are exactly the primitive vectors of norm \(-2\) or \(-4\) satisfying the integrality condition of Definition 49.3. For a short root, \(2\beta_L(v,L)\iscontainedin 2\ZZ = v^2\ZZ\) holds automatically, and \(s_v(x) = x + \beta_L(v,x)\,v\). For a norm \(-4\) vector, integrality requires \(\beta_L(v,L)\iscontainedin 2\ZZ\), which is precisely the condition \(\div_L(v) = 2\); then \(s_v(x) = x + \tfrac12\beta_L(v,x)\,v\) lies in \(\Orth(L)\).


Theorem 49.6 (The two root types exhaust the roots) Let \(L\) be an even \(2\)-elementary lattice and let \(v\in L\) satisfy \(v^2 < 0\). Then \(s_v\in\Orth(L)\) if and only if either \(v^2 = -2\), or \(v^2 = -4\) and \(\div_L(v) = 2\). The list of Definition 49.4 is therefore exhaustive, not merely a selection of two convenient cases.


Proof. This is (Alexeev 2022, sec. 2); that the two conditions are sufficient is Remark 49.5, and the content of the theorem is that no other norm occurs. For \(L\) \(2\)-elementary one has \(\div_L(v)\in\theset{1, 2}\), so the integrality condition \(2\div_L(v)/v^2\in\ZZ\) of Definition 49.3 restricts \(v^2\) to \(\theset{-2, -4}\), with \(\div_L(v) = 2\) forced in the second case.
crumbs: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg's algorithm

title: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg’s algorithm
text:
49.3 Coroots and the weight space

Definition 49.7 Let \(R \definedas \generators{\Phi}_\ZZ\) be a root lattice generated by a root system \(\Phi = \theset{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n}\). The dual lattice \(\dualof{R}\) is called the weight lattice of \(R\), and the dual-basis elements \(\omega_i\) determined by \((\omega_i, \alpha_j) = \delta_{ij}\) are the fundamental weights.


Remark 49.8 For the unimodular root lattice \(E_8\) one has \(\dualof{E_8}\cong E_8\), and the fundamental weights \(\omega_1,\dots,\omega_8\) — the dual basis to the simple roots — have coordinates in the simple-root basis given by the rows of the inverse Gram matrix. The coroots are \(\dualof{\alpha_i} = 2\alpha_i/(\alpha_i,\alpha_i)\), which for the simply-laced \(E_8\) coincide with the simple roots themselves — distinct from the \(\omega_i\).
crumbs: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg's algorithm

title: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg’s algorithm
text:
49.4 Hyperbolic lattices and their polytopes

Definition 49.9 
Let \(L\) be a hyperbolic lattice and \(C_L^+\) one connected component of its positive cone \(C_L\). The intersection pairing induces a hyperbolic metric on \(L_\RR\), and the associated hyperbolic \(n\)-space \(\HH^n_L\) admits two standard models:

the unit hyperboloid model \[
\HH^n_L \definedas \theset{ v\in L_\RR \mid v^2 = 1,\ v\in C_L^+ }
;
\]
the projective (Klein) model \[
\BB^n_L \definedas \PP(C_L) \subset \PP(L_\RR)
,
\] the image of the positive cone in projective space.

In the projective model the boundary \(\partial\HH^n_L\) is the image \(\PP(\theset{v\in L_\RR \mid v^2 = 0})\) of the isotropic cone, geodesics are straight line segments, and angles are distorted. The Poincaré ball and upper half-space charts are the two standard conformal models, in which dihedral angles agree with the angles between the bounding hyperplanes and geodesics are circular arcs meeting the boundary sphere orthogonally.
The hyperbolic distance between points is recovered from the form: for \(v, w\in C_L^+\), \[
\cosh d\!\left([v],[w]\right) = \frac{\beta_L(v,w)}{\sqrt{v^2\,w^2}}
,
\] the right-hand side being at least \(1\) by the reverse Cauchy–Schwarz inequality on the positive cone, with equality exactly when \([v] = [w]\). On the unit hyperboloid, where \(v^2 = w^2 = 1\), this reads \(\cosh d(v,w) = \beta_L(v,w)\).
To a vector \(v\) with \(v^2 < 0\) we associate the hyperplane \(H_v \definedas v^{\perp}\intersect \HH^n_L\). Taking \(v,w\) to be unit normals of \(H_v, H_w\), the relative position of two hyperplanes is governed by the pairing \(v\cdot w \definedas \beta_L(v,w)\):

\(|v\cdot w| < 1\): the hyperplanes meet in the interior of \(\HH^n_L\), at dihedral angle \(\theta\) with \(-v\cdot w = \cos\theta\);
\(|v\cdot w| = 1\): the hyperplanes are asymptotically parallel, meeting at an ideal point of the boundary \(\partial\HH^n_L\);
\(|v\cdot w| > 1\): the hyperplanes are ultra-parallel (divergent), at distance \(d\) with \(-v\cdot w = \cosh d\).

title: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg’s algorithm
text:
49.5 Coxeter groups and Coxeter polytopes

Definition 49.10 A Coxeter group is a group given by a presentation \[
W = \generators{\, s_1,\dots,s_n \mid s_i^2 = e,\ (s_i s_j)^{m_{ij}} = e \,}
,
\] where \(m_{ii} = 1\) and \(m_{ij} = m_{ji}\in\theset{2,3,\dots}\union\theset{\infty}\) for \(i\neq j\), the relation \((s_i s_j)^{m_{ij}} = e\) being imposed only when \(m_{ij} < \infty\). Writing \(S = \theset{s_1,\dots,s_n}\) for the generating set, the pair \((W,S)\) is the associated Coxeter system, and \((m_{ij})\) is its Coxeter matrix (Definition 50.2).


Definition 49.11 
A Coxeter polytope \(P\) in \(X = \EE^n\), \(S^n\), or \(\HH^n\) is a polytope such that:

each face lies in a hyperplane \(H_i \definedas \alpha_i^{\perp}\);
the dihedral angles between adjacent faces are \(\pi/m_{ij}\) for integers \(m_{ij}\geq 2\); and
the reflection group \(W = \generators{ s_{\alpha_i} }\) acts properly discontinuously on \(X\) with fundamental domain \(P\).

section: 49.6 The discriminant locus and Weyl chambers
text:
49.6 The discriminant locus and Weyl chambers

Definition 49.12 The discriminant locus \(\Delta(L)\) is the union of all mirrors, i.e. the hyperplanes orthogonal to the short roots \(\Phi_2(L) = \theset{ v\in L \mid v^2 = -2 }\): \[
\Delta(L) \definedas \Union_{v\in\Phi_2(L)} v^{\perp L}
.
\]


Definition 49.13 The Weyl chambers of \(L\) are the connected components of \[
C_L^{\circ} \definedas C_L \sm \Delta(L)
,
\] where \(C_L\) is the cone of positive-norm vectors. A simple system is a set of roots whose mirrors form the bounding hyperplanes of a single Weyl chamber, i.e. a fundamental domain for the action of the \(2\)-Weyl group \(W^2(L)\) generated by the \((-2)\)-reflections.

title: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg’s algorithm
text:
49.8 Elliptic and parabolic subdiagrams

Definition 49.15 Let \(G\) be a Coxeter–Vinberg diagram with vertices the simple roots \(v_i\). A subdiagram \(D\iscontainedin G\) is:

elliptic if its Gram matrix \((v_i\cdot v_j)\) is negative definite; such a subdiagram defines a finite face of the Coxeter polytope;
parabolic if the Gram matrix of each of its connected components is negative semidefinite with a one-dimensional kernel;
hyperbolic if its Gram matrix is nondegenerate of signature \((1, k-1)\), where \(k\) is the number of vertices of \(D\).

The signs follow the algebraic-geometry convention of this monograph, in which roots have negative norm; in the normalization by roots of norm \(+2\) the three conditions read positive definite, positive semidefinite of corank one, and signature \((k-1,1)\).


Definition 49.16 A parabolic subdiagram is maximal if it is not properly contained in a larger parabolic subdiagram.
Let \(L\) have signature \((2,n)\), let \(I\subset L\) be a primitive isotropic line, and let \(\overline{L}_I \definedas I^{\perp L}/I\) be the hyperbolic lattice at the \(0\)-cusp \([I]\). The maximal parabolic subdiagrams of the Coxeter–Vinberg diagram of a fundamental chamber for a reflection group acting on \(\overline{L}_I\) correspond bijectively to the primitive isotropic lines of \(\overline{L}_I\) met by that chamber, that is, to the rank-\(2\) primitive isotropic sublattices \(J\subseteq L\) containing \(I\); passing to orbits under the stabilizer of \(I\) in the arithmetic group gives the \(1\)-cusps adjacent to the \(0\)-cusp \([I]\) in the Baily–Borel compactification.


Remark 49.17 The bijection is the vertex correspondence of Proposition 52.6: a maximal parabolic subdiagram of rank \(n-1\) is cut out by the walls through an ideal vertex of the chamber, and that ideal vertex is the isotropic line spanned by the radical of the subdiagram.

title: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg’s algorithm
text:
49.9 Vinberg’s algorithm

Theorem 49.18 (Vinberg’s algorithm for a fundamental chamber) Let \(\Gamma\iscontainedin\Orth(L)\) be an arithmetic reflection subgroup of a hyperbolic lattice \(L\). Vinberg’s algorithm constructs a fundamental chamber \(P\iscontainedin\HH^n\) for \(\Gamma\) as follows (Vinberg 1975).

Control vector. Choose a generic positive-norm vector \(v_0\in C_L^+\). Its stabilizer in \(\Gamma\) is the reflection group of the finite subdiagram of roots orthogonal to \(v_0\), which are used as the first walls.
Enumeration by height. Seek primitive vectors \(v\in L\) with \(v^2 < 0\), \(s_v\in\Gamma\), and mirror \(H_v\) meeting the current cone \(\tilde P\). Order the candidate roots by increasing height \[
h(v) \definedas \frac{-2\,(v_0\cdot v)}{v^2}
,
\] a quantity monotone in the hyperbolic distance from \(v_0\) to \(H_v\) (for roots of a given norm), used to order the candidate roots and process them in successive batches of increasing height.
Acceptance / pruning. A candidate root \(v\) at the current height is kept only if its mirror bounds the chamber on the side containing \(v_0\); equivalently, the inward normals of accepted walls pair non-negatively, so \(v\) is accepted iff \(v\cdot r_i \geq 0\) for every previously accepted root \(r_i\) (a mirror with some \(v\cdot r_i < 0\) would cut into the interior of \(\tilde P\)). Roots whose hyperplanes do not bound \(\tilde P\) are discarded.
Diagram. The algorithm proceeds until \(\tilde P\) becomes a convex polytope of finite volume. The Gram matrix of the accepted simple roots then determines the Coxeter–Vinberg diagram of \(P\) (Definition 49.14).

The algorithm terminates in finitely many steps if and only if \(\Gamma\) has finite covolume in \(\Orth(L)\).


Remark 49.19 The source note states step 3 as “discard those roots whose hyperplanes do not intersect \(\tilde P\) transversely”; the explicit inequality \(v\cdot r_i\geq 0\) recorded above is Vinberg’s acceptance criterion for that condition in the algebraic-geometry sign convention (Vinberg 1975).


Definition 49.20 (Lannér subgraph) A Lannér subgraph of a Coxeter–Vinberg diagram is a minimal non-parabolic subdiagram whose Coxeter group acts on hyperbolic space with a fundamental polyhedron of finite volume; equivalently, a diagram all of whose proper subdiagrams are elliptic but which is not itself elliptic or parabolic.


Theorem 49.21 (A sufficient criterion for completeness) Let \(\Gamma\) be a Coxeter–Vinberg diagram without dotted edges, obtained from a run of Theorem 49.18. If \(\Gamma\) contains no Lannér subgraph, and every connected parabolic subdiagram of \(\Gamma\) is contained in a maximal parabolic subdiagram of maximal rank, then \(\Gamma\) is complete: the accepted roots bound a finite-volume polytope and the algorithm may be stopped.


Proof. This is the sufficient condition of (Vinberg 1975), in the form used in (Alexeev 2022, sec. 3).


Remark 49.22 The criterion is what makes a run of Vinberg’s algorithm into a proof rather than a computation that has not yet terminated: without it, the algorithm has produced a chamber that might still acquire further walls at greater height. It applies only in the absence of dotted edges, that is when no two walls of the chamber are ultra-parallel; for the diagrams on the line \(r + a = 22\) this is the case, and Theorem 53.11 records the resulting diagrams.

title: 49  Hyperbolic reflection groups and Vinberg’s algorithm
text:
49.10 Root-system conventions and tables

Remark 49.23 (Bourbaki conventions and twists) The classical root systems are taken with the Bourbaki labeling, in the negative-definite twists appropriate to the algebraic-geometry convention: \[
A_n(-1),\quad B_n(-2),\quad C_n(-1),\quad D_n(-1),\quad
E_n(-1)\ (n\in\theset{6,7,8}),\quad F_4(-2),\quad G_2(-1)
.
\] Both the simply-laced systems \(A_n, D_n, E_n\) and the non-simply-laced systems \(B_n, C_n, F_4, G_2\) occur. The Coxeter diagrams and Gram matrices used throughout are derived from these conventions; the ranks, root counts, Weyl groups, discriminant groups, and explicit Euclidean basis constructions are collected in the root-lattice tables of the Root Systems section and the Diagrams appendix.

Vinberg, E. B. 1975. “Some Arithmetical Discrete Groups in Lobachevskii Spaces.” In Discrete Subgroups of Lie Groups and Applications to Moduli. Oxford University Press.

title: 50  Coxeter systems and their classification
text:
Definition 50.2 Let \(S\) be a finite set. A Coxeter matrix on \(S\) is a symmetric matrix \(M = (m_{st})_{s,t\in S}\) with \[
m_{ss} = 1,
\qquad
m_{st} = m_{ts} \in \theset{2,3,4,\dots}\union\theset{\infty}
\quad (s\neq t)
.
\] The Coxeter group presented by \(M\) is the group \(W(M)\) of Definition 49.10, the relation \((s t)^{m_{st}} = e\) being imposed only for \(m_{st} < \infty\). The pair \((W(M), S)\) is a Coxeter system of rank \(\abs{S}\). Its Coxeter diagram \(\Sigma(M)\) is the graph on the vertex set \(S\) with an edge \(\theset{s,t}\) whenever \(m_{st}\geq 3\), labelled by \(m_{st}\) when \(m_{st}\geq 4\).


Definition 50.3 (The Gram form of a Coxeter matrix) Let \(M\) be a Coxeter matrix on \(S\). The Gram form of \(M\) is the symmetric bilinear form \(G(M)\) on the real vector space \(\RR^S\) with basis \(\theset{\alpha_s}_{s\in S}\) determined by \[
G(M)_{st} \definedas \beta(\alpha_s,\alpha_t) = 2\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{m_{st}}\right)
,
\] read on the diagonal as \(G(M)_{ss} = 2\cos\pi = -2\), and as \(G(M)_{st} = 2\) when \(m_{st} = \infty\). Each \(\alpha_s\) has norm \(-2\) and is therefore a short root in the sense of Definition 49.4; the reflections \(s_{\alpha_s}\) of Definition 49.2 preserve \(G(M)\), and \(s\mapsto s_{\alpha_s}\) extends to an injective homomorphism \(W(M)\to \Orth(\RR^S, G(M))\) (Bourbaki 2008; Humphreys 1990).


Remark 50.4 (Normalized pairings) Dividing by the norms recovers the quantity that labels the edges of a Coxeter–Vinberg diagram: with \(\alpha_s^2 = \alpha_t^2 = -2\), \[
g_{st} = \frac{\beta(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)}{\sqrt{\alpha_s^2\,\alpha_t^2}}
= \frac{G(M)_{st}}{2}
= \cos\!\left(\frac{\pi}{m_{st}}\right)
,
\] which is the normalization of Definition 49.14. A Coxeter matrix produces only the values \(g_{st}\leq 1\); Vinberg’s diagrams admit in addition the ultraparallel case \(g_{st} > 1\), which corresponds to no finite \(m_{st}\) and is drawn dotted.


Remark 50.5 (The values at small orders) \[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
m & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & \infty \\\hline
2\cos(\pi/m) & 0 & 1 & \sqrt2 & \dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2} & \sqrt3 & 2
\end{array}
\]


Remark 50.6 (Gram and Cartan matrices) Let \(\theset{\alpha_s}_{s\in S}\) be simple roots in a lattice \(L\). Two matrices are attached to them. The Gram matrix is \(G_{st} = \beta_L(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)\); it is symmetric and records the form. The Cartan matrix is \[
A_{st} \definedas \frac{2\,\beta_L(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)}{\beta_L(\alpha_t,\alpha_t)}
,
\] so that \(A_{ss} = 2\) and \(s_{\alpha_t}(\alpha_s) = \alpha_s - A_{st}\alpha_t\); it records the reflections and is symmetric only when all the \(\alpha_s\) have equal norm. The two are related by a diagonal factor on the right, \[
A = G\cdot\diag\!\left(\frac{2}{G_{11}},\dots,\frac{2}{G_{nn}}\right),
\qquad
G = A\cdot\diag\!\left(\frac{G_{11}}{2},\dots,\frac{G_{nn}}{2}\right)
,
\] so \(G\) is the Cartan matrix symmetrized by the root lengths. In the simply-laced case, where every \(\alpha_s^2 = -2\), one has \(A = -G\). When two root lengths occur the two matrices record different data: for \(\alpha_s^2 = -2\) and \(\alpha_t^2 = -4\) with \(\beta_L(\alpha_s,\alpha_t) = 2\), the Cartan entries are \(A_{st} = 1\) and \(A_{ts} = 2\).


Remark 50.7 (The opposite normalization) Much of the reflection-group literature normalizes simple roots to \(\alpha_s^2 = +2\) and attaches to \(M\) the Schläfli matrix \(C_{st} = -2\cos(\pi/m_{st})\), with \(C_{ss} = 2\). Then \(C = -G(M)\), and every definiteness statement below is read with the opposite sign: a spherical system has \(C\) positive definite.

title: 50  Coxeter systems and their classification
text:
50.2 Classification by definiteness

Definition 50.8 Let \((W,S)\) be an irreducible Coxeter system of rank \(n\) with Coxeter matrix \(M\) and Gram form \(G = G(M)\). Say that \((W,S)\), or \(M\), is

spherical if \(G\) is negative definite;
euclidean if \(G\) is negative semidefinite and \(\ker G\) has rank \(1\);
hyperbolic if \(G\) is nondegenerate of signature \((1, n-1)\).

A Gram form of signature \((p,q)\) with \(p\geq 2\) falls under none of the three.
For subdiagrams, Definition 49.15 names the corresponding conditions elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic. An elliptic subdiagram is one all of whose components are spherical; a parabolic subdiagram on \(k\) vertices with \(c\) connected components has kernel of rank \(c\), hence rank \(k-c\).


Remark 50.9 By Sylvester’s law of inertia, invoked in the Lattice Theory section to define the signature, the numbers \(n_+\) and \(n_-\) of positive and negative squares in a diagonalization of \(G\) over \(\RR\), and the rank of \(\ker G\), are independent of the basis. The three conditions of Definition 50.8 are therefore properties of the form \(G\) rather than of the matrix representing it: spherical is \((n_+,n_-) = (0,n)\), euclidean is \((0,n-1)\) with a one-dimensional kernel, and hyperbolic is \((1,n-1)\).


Theorem 50.10 (The geometry of the three types) 
Let \((W,S)\) be an irreducible Coxeter system of rank \(n\) with Gram form \(G\).

\((W,S)\) is spherical if and only if \(W\) is finite. In that case \(W\) acts on the unit sphere of the negative definite space \((\RR^S, -G)\) as a finite reflection group whose fundamental domain is a spherical simplex (Bourbaki 2008; Humphreys 1990).
\((W,S)\) is euclidean if and only if \(W\) is infinite and admits a faithful action on a euclidean space \(\EE^{\,n-1}\) as a discrete group generated by \(n\) affine reflections, with fundamental domain a euclidean simplex (Bourbaki 2008; Humphreys 1990).
If \((W,S)\) is hyperbolic, then \(\RR^S\) with the form \(G\) is a model of hyperbolic \((n-1)\)-space in the sense of Definition 49.9, and the reflections \(s_{\alpha_s}\) generate a discrete subgroup of its isometry group whose fundamental domain is the Coxeter polytope \[
P \definedas \theset{\, [v] \in \HH^{\,n-1} \mid \beta(v,\alpha_s)\geq 0 \text{ for all } s\in S \,}
\] of Definition 49.11 (Vinberg 1967; Vinberg 1985).



Remark 50.11 Statement (3) asserts nothing about the volume of \(P\): the finite-volume and compact cases are separated by the criterion of Theorem 52.10.

title: 50  Coxeter systems and their classification
section: 50.3 Subdiagrams and the inheritance of signature
text:
50.3 Subdiagrams and the inheritance of signature

Definition 50.12 Let \(\Sigma\) be the Coxeter diagram of \((W,S)\) and let \(I\iscontainedin S\). The subdiagram \(\Sigma_I\) is the induced diagram on \(I\), with Coxeter matrix \(M[I,I]\) and Gram form the principal submatrix \(G[I,I]\). The rank of \(\Sigma_I\) is the rank of \(G[I,I]\). The subgroup \[
W_I \definedas \generators{\, s \mid s\in I \,} \leq W
\] is the standard parabolic subgroup determined by \(I\), and \((W_I, I)\) is a Coxeter system with Coxeter matrix \(M[I,I]\) (Bourbaki 2008).


Remark 50.13 (Parabolic subgroups and parabolic subdiagrams) The two uses of parabolic are independent. The subgroup \(W_I\) is a standard parabolic subgroup for every subset \(I\iscontainedin S\), whatever the definiteness of \(G[I,I]\). The subdiagram \(\Sigma_I\) is parabolic when each of its connected components is euclidean (Definition 49.15), and then \((W_I, I)\) is a product of irreducible euclidean Coxeter systems, one for each component.


Proposition 50.14 (Restriction cannot increase the positive index) Let \(\beta\) be a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional real vector space \(V\), write \(n_\pm(\beta)\) for its numbers of positive and negative squares, and let \(V'\leq V\) be a subspace of codimension \(c\). Then \[
n_+(\beta) - c \;\leq\; n_+\!\left(\restrictionof{\beta}{V'}\right) \;\leq\; n_+(\beta)
,
\] and the same inequalities hold for \(n_-\).


Proof. The integer \(n_+(\beta)\) is the largest dimension of a subspace of \(V\) on which \(\beta\) is positive definite. A subspace of \(V'\) on which \(\restrictionof{\beta}{V'}\) is positive definite is such a subspace of \(V\), which gives the upper bound. If \(P\leq V\) is positive definite of dimension \(n_+(\beta)\), then \(\beta\) is positive definite on \(P\intersect V'\), and \(\dim(P\intersect V')\geq n_+(\beta) - c\), which gives the lower bound. Applying both to \(-\beta\) gives the statement for \(n_-\).


Corollary 50.15 
Let \(\Sigma\) be a Coxeter diagram on \(S\) and \(J\iscontainedin I\iscontainedin S\).

If \(\Sigma_I\) is elliptic then so is \(\Sigma_J\). Equivalently, a subdiagram that is not elliptic is contained in no elliptic subdiagram.
If the Gram form of \(\Sigma\) has exactly one positive square — in particular if \(\Sigma\) is hyperbolic — then the Gram form of every subdiagram of \(\Sigma\) has at most one positive square, so every subdiagram is negative semidefinite or of signature \((1,q)\) with a possibly nontrivial kernel.



Proof. For (1), the restriction of a negative definite form to a subspace is negative definite. For (2), apply the upper bound of Proposition 50.14 with \(n_+(G) = 1\).


Remark 50.16 Part (1) is what makes an enumeration of the elliptic subdiagrams of a Coxeter–Vinberg diagram tractable: a subset that fails to be elliptic can be discarded together with all subsets containing it, so the search runs over the order ideal of elliptic subsets rather than over all of \(2^{S}\).

title: 50  Coxeter systems and their classification
text:
50.4 The spherical and euclidean classifications

Theorem 50.17 (Classification of spherical Coxeter systems) An irreducible Coxeter system is spherical if and only if its Coxeter diagram is one of \[
A_n\ (n\geq 1),\quad
B_n\ (n\geq 2),\quad
D_n\ (n\geq 4),\quad
E_6,\ E_7,\ E_8,\quad
F_4,\quad
H_3,\quad
H_4,\quad
I_2(p)\ (p\geq 5)
,
\] and diagrams from distinct entries of this list are not isomorphic (Bourbaki 2008; Humphreys 1990).


Remark 50.18 Here \(I_2(p)\) denotes the rank-two diagram with \(m_{12} = p\), so that \(I_2(3)\cong A_2\), \(I_2(4)\cong B_2\) and \(I_2(6)\cong G_2\); the list above records each isomorphism class once. The root systems \(B_n\) and \(C_n\) of Definition 36.11 have the same Coxeter matrix and so contribute a single entry, the two being distinguished by their root lengths rather than by their Coxeter system.


Theorem 50.19 (Classification of euclidean Coxeter systems) An irreducible Coxeter system is euclidean if and only if its Coxeter diagram is one of \[
\tilde A_1,\quad
\tilde A_n\ (n\geq 2),\quad
\tilde B_n\ (n\geq 3),\quad
\tilde C_n\ (n\geq 2),\quad
\tilde D_n\ (n\geq 4),\quad
\tilde E_6,\ \tilde E_7,\ \tilde E_8,\quad
\tilde F_4,\quad
\tilde G_2
,
\] each of rank \(n+1\) and drawn in the diagram table of the Diagrams appendix (Bourbaki 2008). The diagram \(\tilde A_1\) has two vertices joined by a bond with \(m_{12} = \infty\), and \(\tilde A_n\) for \(n\geq 2\) is the cycle on \(n+1\) vertices with all bonds \(m_{ij} = 3\).


Proposition 50.20 (The radical of a euclidean diagram) Let \(\Sigma\) be an irreducible euclidean diagram on the vertex set \(I\), with Gram form \(G[I,I]\) and simple roots \(\theset{\alpha_s}_{s\in I}\). Then \(\ker G[I,I]\) is spanned by a vector \[
\delta = \Sum_{s\in I} n_s\,\alpha_s
\qquad\text{with all } n_s > 0
,
\] unique up to scalar, and \(\delta^2 = 0\) (Bourbaki 2008; Humphreys 1990).


Remark 50.21 The positivity of the coefficients \(n_s\) is what places \(\delta\) in the closure of a cone rather than merely in the kernel of a form, and is the reason a parabolic subdiagram of a hyperbolic Coxeter polytope determines an ideal point of the boundary rather than an arbitrary isotropic line; see Proposition 52.6. For \(\tilde E_8\) the coefficients are the marks \((1,2,3,4,6,5,4,3,2)\) of the highest root of \(E_8\).
crumbs: 50  Coxeter systems and their classification

title: 50  Coxeter systems and their classification
text:
50.5 Crystallographic Coxeter systems

Definition 50.22 A Coxeter matrix \(M\) on \(S\) is crystallographic if \(m_{st}\in\theset{2,3,4,6,\infty}\) for all \(s\neq t\).


Theorem 50.23 A Coxeter matrix \(M\) is crystallographic if and only if the group \(W(M)\) preserves a lattice of full rank in \(\RR^S\) (Bourbaki 2008; Humphreys 1990).


Example 50.24 (Rescaling to an integral form) The equal-norm normalization \(\alpha_s^2 = -2\) of Definition 50.3 does not itself make the form integral, and a crystallographic \(M\) becomes integral only after the simple roots are rescaled. For \(m_{st} = 4\) one has \(\beta(\alpha_s,\alpha_t) = 2\cos(\pi/4) = \sqrt2\); replacing \(\alpha_t\) by \(\alpha_t' \definedas \sqrt2\,\alpha_t\) gives \[
\alpha_s^2 = -2,
\qquad
(\alpha_t')^2 = -4,
\qquad
\beta(\alpha_s,\alpha_t') = 2
,
\] a short root and a long root in the sense of Definition 49.4. For \(m_{st} = 6\) the same rescaling by \(\sqrt3\) gives norms \(-2\) and \(-6\) with pairing \(3\), which is the ratio occurring in \(G_2\). For \(m_{st}\in\theset{2,3}\) the entries \(0\) and \(1\) are already integral, and the simply-laced diagrams need no rescaling.


Definition 50.25 Let \(M\) be a Coxeter matrix on \(S\). Its base field is the subfield \[
K(M) \definedas \QQ\!\left(\, 2\cos(\pi/m_{st}) \;:\; s\neq t,\ m_{st} < \infty \,\right) \iscontainedin \RR
,
\] the smallest field over which the Gram form \(G(M)\) is defined.


Proposition 50.26 For an integer \(m\geq 2\) one has \(2\cos(\pi/m) = \zeta_{2m} + \inverseof{\zeta_{2m}}\) for a primitive \(2m\)-th root of unity \(\zeta_{2m}\), so \(\QQ(2\cos(\pi/m))\) is the maximal totally real subfield of \(\QQ(\zeta_{2m})\) and \[
\left[\QQ\!\left(2\cos(\pi/m)\right) : \QQ\right] = \tfrac12\,\#\unitsof{(\ZZ/2m\ZZ)}
.
\] In particular \(K(M) = \QQ\) exactly when \(m_{st}\in\theset{2,3,\infty}\) for all \(s\neq t\).


Proposition 50.27 (When the Gram form is integral) \(G(M)\) has all its entries in \(\ZZ\) if and only if \(m_{st}\in\theset{2,3,\infty}\) for every \(s\neq t\). Among the Coxeter matrices with every \(m_{st}\) finite, these are exactly the simply-laced ones.


Proof. The entries are the values of Remark 50.5, and an entry lies in \(\ZZ\) only if it lies in \(\QQ\). By Proposition 50.26 the degree of \(\QQ(2\cos(\pi/m))\) over \(\QQ\) is \(\tfrac12\#(\ZZ/2m\ZZ)^\times\), which equals \(1\) exactly when \(2m\in\theset{4,6}\), that is when \(m\in\theset{2,3}\); the value at \(m=\infty\) is \(2\). The remaining orders therefore give irrational entries, and the three admissible orders give \(0\), \(1\) and \(2\).


Example 50.28 (The non-crystallographic spherical types) Of the spherical types of Theorem 50.17, those that are not crystallographic are \(H_3\), \(H_4\), and \(I_2(p)\) for \(p\notin\theset{2,3,4,6}\).
For \(m = 5\), \[
2\cos(\pi/5) = \varphi \definedas \frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},
\qquad
\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1
,
\] so \(H_3\) and \(H_4\) both have base field \(K = \QQ(\sqrt5)\), and their Gram forms have entries in the ring of integers \(\ZZ[\varphi]\) of that field. For \(m = 8\) the base field is \(\QQ(\sqrt{2+\sqrt2})\), of degree \(4\) over \(\QQ\) by Proposition 50.26.


Remark 50.29 (Galois conjugates of a Gram form) Let \(M\) be a Coxeter matrix with base field \(K = K(M)\), a totally real number field, and let \(\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(K/\QQ)\). Applying \(\sigma\) entrywise to \(G(M)\) produces a symmetric \(K\)-valued form \(\sigma(G(M))\) of the same rank, with the same diagonal \(-2\). Its signature is not determined by that of \(G(M)\): the signature of a symmetric form over a totally real field is not a Galois invariant, as the rank-one forms \(\generators{1-\sqrt2}\) and \(\generators{1+\sqrt2}\) over \(\QQ(\sqrt2)\) show. Whether every nontrivial conjugate of a hyperbolic Gram form is negative definite is a condition on \(M\) that must be computed, and is the arithmeticity question recorded in the Open Problems section.

title: 50  Coxeter systems and their classification
text:
50.6 Origins

Remark 50.30 (Attribution) Coxeter introduced the matrices and diagrams now named after him and classified the finite reflection groups, obtaining the list of Theorem 50.17 with its two non-crystallographic exceptional types \(H_3\) and \(H_4\); the euclidean classification of Theorem 50.19 grew out of Weyl’s theory of root systems and the affine reflection groups. Both are given in Bourbaki (Bourbaki 2008) and in Humphreys (Humphreys 1990), and the geometric and topological theory of general Coxeter groups in Davis (Davis 2008). The hyperbolic theory — the polytope picture, the finite-volume criterion, and the algorithm of Theorem 49.18 — is due to Vinberg (Vinberg 1967; Vinberg 1975; Vinberg 1985); Lannér classified the compact hyperbolic Coxeter simplices, and Vinberg and Kaplinskaja determined the reflection groups of the odd unimodular hyperbolic lattices \(\latI_{18,1}\) and \(\latI_{19,1}\) (Vinberg and Kaplinskaja 1978), which are the ranks the moduli theory of this monograph meets.

title: 51  Foldings of Dynkin diagrams
51  Foldings of Dynkin diagrams
section: 51.2 Folded roots and folded root systems
text:
51.2 Folded roots and folded root systems

Definition 51.3 (Folded root systems) Let \(L\) be a lattice containing a root system \(\Phi\) and \(G \subset \Orth(L)\) a finite group preserving \(\Phi\). Given a simple root \(\alpha_i \in \Phi\), let \([\alpha_i] \subset \Phi\) denote its \(G\)-orbit.
The associated folded root and folded root system are defined by \[
\beta_{[\alpha_i]} \definedas \Sum_{\alpha_j \in [\alpha_i]} \alpha_j \in L^G,
\qquad
\Phi^G \definedas \theset{ \beta_{[\alpha_i]} \in L^G \mid [\alpha_i] \in \Phi/G }
.
\]
Each folded root corresponds to a folded node in the Dynkin diagram. For an involution \(I\), \(\beta_{[\alpha_i]} = \alpha_i + I(\alpha_i) \in L^G\).

title: 51  Foldings of Dynkin diagrams
text:
51.3 Examples

Example 51.4 (Examples of classical foldings) Folding produces scaled root systems in the invariant lattice \(L^G\). Explicit examples computed via Definition 51.3:

\(A_5 \to B_3(2)\): under horizontal reflection (\(G = S_2\)), \(\Phi(A_5^G)\) has Gram matrix \(G_{B_3(2)} = 2 \cdot G_{B_3} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\) (norms \(4, 4, 2\): two long, one short).
\(D_4 \to C_3\): under vertical reflection (\(G = S_2\)), \(\Phi(D_4^G)\) has Gram matrix equal to \(G_{C_3}\).
\(D_4 \to G_2\): under rotation by \(2\pi/3\) (\(G = \ZZ/3\ZZ\)), \(\Phi(D_4^G)\) has Gram matrix equal to \(G_{G_2}\).
\(E_6 \to F_4(2)\): under horizontal reflection (\(G = S_2\)), \(\Phi(E_6^G)\) has Gram matrix equal to \(G_{F_4(2)}\).

Here the scaling notation \(B_3(2)\) and \(F_4(2)\) records that the invariant-lattice Gram matrix equals the corresponding root-system Gram matrix rescaled by \(2\). (These Gram matrices are written in the standard positive-definite normalization; negate for the AG convention of Definition 36.2.)

title: 51  Foldings of Dynkin diagrams
text:
51.4 The root-folding criterion for \(T_\dP\)
The criterion below is stated in terms of the short and long roots of \(T_\dP\): \(\Phi^2\) denotes the short roots (norm \(-2\)) and \(\Phi^4\) the long roots (norm \(-4\) with divisor \(2\)), in the \(k\)-root sense of the root systems material.

Lemma 51.5 (Root folding criterion) 
Let \(\Phi(T_\dP)\) be the root system of \(T_\dP\) and \(I = -I_\En\) the induced involution on \(T_\dP\) whose fixed lattice is \(\ten\).
The folded roots \(\beta_{[v]} \in \Phi\left( T_\dP^{\generators{I}} \right)\) arise in exactly one of the following ways:

\(v \in \Phi^2(T_\dP)\) and \(\beta_{[v]} \in \Phi(\ten)\);
\(v \in \Phi^4(T_\dP)\) and \(\beta_{[v]} \in \Phi(\ten)\); or
\(v \in \Phi^2(T_\dP) \intersect I(v)^{\perp T_\dP}\), and so \(\beta_{[v]} \definedas v + I(v) \in \Phi^4(\ten)\) is the sum of orthogonal roots in \(\Phi^2(T_\dP)\).


This criterion governs how roots in the boundary lattices at the \(0\)-cusps of \(F_{(2,2,0)}\) descend or combine when passing to the \(I\)-invariant sublattices corresponding to \(\fentwo\).

title: 51  Foldings of Dynkin diagrams
text:
51.5 Mirror moves

Definition 51.6 (Mirror moves) A mirror move is a lattice-theoretic operation governed by the existence of a primitive isotropic vector \(\eta \in T\) of a specified type and splitting:

Odd/simple: \(\operatorname{div}_T(\eta) = 1\), splitting as \(T \cong U \oplus K\). The new invariants are \((r-2, a, 1)\).
Even, ordinary: \(\operatorname{div}_T(\eta) = 2\) and \(\eta^*\) is ordinary, splitting as \(T \cong U(2) \oplus K\). The new invariants are \((r-2, a-2, 1)\).
Even, characteristic: \(\operatorname{div}_T(\eta) = 2\) and \(\eta^*\) is characteristic, splitting as \(T \cong I_{1,1}(2) \oplus K\). The new invariants are \((r-2, a-2, 0)\).

The move replaces \(T\) with \(\overline{T}_\eta = \eta^{\perp T}/\eta\), navigating Nikulin’s pyramid of \(2\)-elementary lattices to compute cusp diagrams when \(\Gamma = \Orth^+(T)\).

text: 52.1 The Tits cone
crumbs: 52  Hyperbolic Coxeter polytopes and finite covolume

title: 52  Hyperbolic Coxeter polytopes and finite covolume
text:
Definition 52.2 Let \((W,S)\) be a Coxeter system with Gram form \(G\) on \(V \definedas \RR^S\) and simple roots \(\theset{\alpha_s}_{s\in S}\), and let \(W\) act on the dual space \(V^*\) by the contragredient of its action on \(V\). The closed fundamental chamber is \[
\overline{C} \definedas \theset{\, f\in V^* \mid f(\alpha_s)\geq 0 \text{ for all } s\in S \,}
,
\] and the Tits cone of \((W,S)\) is \[
U \definedas \Union_{w\in W} w\!\left(\overline{C}\right) \iscontainedin V^*
.
\] When \(G\) is nondegenerate it identifies \(V\) with \(V^*\), and \(\overline C\) becomes the cone \(\theset{v\in V \mid \beta(v,\alpha_s)\geq 0}\) over the closure of a Weyl chamber in the sense of Definition 49.13.


Theorem 52.3 (Properties of the Tits cone) Let \((W,S)\), \(\overline C\) and \(U\) be as in Definition 52.2, and for \(f\in \overline C\) write \(I(f) \definedas \theset{s\in S \mid f(\alpha_s) = 0}\).

\(U\) is a convex cone, and \(\overline{C}\) is a strict fundamental domain for the action of \(W\) on \(U\): every \(W\)-orbit in \(U\) meets \(\overline{C}\) in exactly one point.
The stabilizer of \(f\in\overline{C}\) in \(W\) is the standard parabolic subgroup \(W_{I(f)}\) of Definition 50.12.
A point \(f\in\overline{C}\) lies in the interior of \(U\) if and only if \(W_{I(f)}\) is finite, that is, if and only if the subdiagram \(\Sigma_{I(f)}\) is elliptic.
\(W\) acts properly discontinuously on the interior of \(U\).

These are theorems of Tits, recorded in (Bourbaki 2008; Humphreys 1990).


Remark 52.4 For a spherical Coxeter system \(U = V^*\). For an irreducible euclidean one, with \(\ker G = \RR\delta\) as in Proposition 50.20, \(U\) is the open half-space \(\theset{f \mid f(\delta) > 0}\) together with the origin, and the affine reflection group of Theorem 50.10(2) is its action on the hyperplane \(f(\delta) = 1\).
For a hyperbolic Coxeter system, part (3) says which points of the chamber have finite stabilizer, and Proposition 52.6 identifies those on the boundary of the cone: an ordinary vertex of the polytope lies in the interior of \(U\), and an ideal vertex does not, its stabilizer being an infinite euclidean reflection group.
